nodes.t: The dead kept in the cave
nodes.s: Neanderthals repeatedly carried their dead into one cave in northern Iraq and put them down in the floor. Shanidar 4 was found on his side with his arm under his head; Shanidar Z lay in a hollow gouged out to fit her, with a stone under her head. The cluster dates to roughly seventy to seventy-five thousand years ago.
nodes.g: The oldest evidence on this site of people treating the dead as somewhere you go, rather than something you leave behind. It sits about fifty-five thousand years before the dog, which settles an argument this site was getting wrong: one-sided attachment to a non-human does not begin with a domesticated animal. It is also the discipline case. The famous flowers were a mistake - the pollen turned out to come from burrowing rodents - and the burials survived the debunk anyway. That is what a real claim looks like after someone has been wrong about part of it. One limit worth stating: Sunghir, later and better studied, shows this was not a single uniform practice, so what Shanidar documents is the earliest *instance* of something that varied a great deal.

src.claim: Dates and method: repeated interment in the same cave; the most recent individual found in a shallow scoop partly covered by rocks that appear to have been placed, dated to around 70,000-75,000 years ago, with an earlier cluster at 70,000-60,000 and others at 45,000-50,000.
src.citation: University of Cambridge, Department of Archaeology. Shanidar Cave Project. Date of access recorded in tools/citation_audit_baseline.json run.

src.claim: The peer-reviewed report of the new articulated remains. Recorded because it is the primary source, and marked unverified because Cambridge Core returns 403 to an unauthenticated request.
src.citation: Pomeroy, E., Bennett, P., & Hunt, C. O. (2020). New Neanderthal remains associated with the 'flower burial' at Shanidar Cave. Antiquity, 94(373), 11-26. doi:10.15184/aqy.2019.207

nodes.s: Upper Paleolithic carvers in Europe made small figures of animals and people from mammoth ivory from about forty thousand years ago. The Vogelherd set includes a cave lion, a bison, a horse, a bear, a mammoth, and a lion-man - a body with a human face on a lion's. At La Madeleine in France a bison carved from antler is caught mid-grooming, turning its head to lick its own side.
nodes.g: This is what the dog entry used to deny. Animals carrying human qualities were being made, kept and shown to other people tens of thousands of years before the dog: the grooming gesture is specifically human, and somebody carved it in antler on purpose. It also puts an anthropomorphised animal on the same taxonomy shelf as the dog roughly twenty-five thousand years ahead of it, which is the honest shape of the argument. The dog is not the first animal to be given human shape in the imagination. It is the first animal to be bred into living alongside us.

src.claim: Animal, human and hybrid figurines made by modern humans beginning at least 35,000 years ago, across a broad area of Europe, in a spread of sizes, shapes and styles made by different groups - including the Vogelherd cave lion, mammoth, bison and horse, and the lion-man.
src.citation: Smithsonian Institution, Human Origins Program. Figurines. Human Evolution Evidence: Behavior, Art & Music.

src.claim: The La Madeleine 'bison licking its side', Magdalenian, c. 14,000 years old, carved from the palmate section of a reindeer antler, shown turning to lick its own flank - a self-grooming gesture rendered in a portable object.
src.citation: Bradshaw Foundation. La Madeleine Bison Licking its Side. Ice Age Art. (Catalogue entry for the carving held at the Musee d'Archéologie Nationale, Saint-Germain-en-Laye.)

nodes.s: At Sunghir on the Russian plain, thirty-four thousand years ago, three burials were lavish with beads and ochre and one was not treated that way at all. People were buried in a site that kept producing them for thousands of years, individually and very differently.
nodes.g: This entry exists to disagree with another one on this site. Shanidar is the earliest evidence of people returning to the dead; Sunghir is the evidence that this was not one practice with one belief behind it. Of the individuals recovered, four were intentionally buried, two had their remains manipulated and one seems to have received little or no formal treatment, and the only thing uniting the three rich burials is the quantity of beads - which the analysis reads as social behaviour in life rather than in death. That is a harder finding than a uniform origin would be, and it is better for this site, because it means the archaeological record cannot be read as a single relationship any more than the later one can. Formicola's case is the memorable one: at Romito Cave an adolescent dwarf was buried together with a woman, underneath an engraving of a bull. A named dead person, put under a named animal, deliberately, thirty thousand years before anything was written down.

src.claim: The finding that complicates a uniform reading: 'the mortuary behaviour evident at Sunghir indicates considerable diversity in their treatment at an individual level. Four of the individuals were intentionally buried, two of them had their remains manipulated and one of them seems to have received little or no formal treatment', with only the abundance of beads uniting the three elaborate burials - 'and that should reflect social behaviour in life, rather than in death'.
src.citation: Trinkaus, E., & Buzhilova, A. P. (2018). Diversity and differential disposal of the dead at Sunghir. Antiquity, 92(361), 7-21.

src.claim: The concrete case the entry turns on, and the framing that Upper Palaeolithic burials are evidence about 'ideological aspects' and 'the perception of diversity and its links to magical-religious beliefs': 'the adolescent dwarf from Romito Cave (Italy), buried together with a woman under the engraving of a bull', alongside the double burial of the Sunghir children and the Dolniestonice triple interment.
src.citation: Formicola, V. (2007). From the Sunghir Children to the Romito Dwarf: Aspects of the Upper Paleolithic Funerary Landscape. Current Anthropology, 48(3), 446-453.

src.claim: Dating and site description from an openable source: the site lies about 200km east of present-day Moscow, was discovered in 1955 while being quarried for gravel, and was excavated from 1957 to 1977; burials include an adult male covered in beads and ochre and a juvenile and an adolescent of about ten and twelve, buried head to head.
src.citation: Surugue, L. (2018, February 22). Why This Paleolithic Burial Site Is So Strange (and So Important). SAPIENS.

nodes.s: A species that has spent fifteen thousand years being selected partly for forming attachment to one particular ape.
nodes.g: The original transparasocial relationship, and the only one that has reliably worked. Everything invented since is a worse version with better latency, and the reason it is compared to this constantly is that the comparison is fair.

src.citation: Parker, H. G., & Gilbert, S. F. (2015). From caveman companion to medical innovator: genomic insights into the origin and evolution of domestic dogs. Advances in Genomics and Genetics, 5, 239-255. doi:10.2147/AGG.S57678
src.claim: The timing is genuinely unsettled and the paper says so rather than rounding it. Fossils more similar to modern dogs date to 14,000-17,000 years ago; whole-genome divergence estimates run 13,000-32,000 years ago and mtDNA anywhere from 5,400 to over 100,000; the authors place the actual domestication 'somewhere in between 15,000 and 30,000 ya'. On what was selected for: the behavioural genes under selection are response to stress, fear and defence, and a reduced fear response is offered as a candidate driver of domestication - not attachment itself. Fox selection experiments are cited as showing phenotypic change is achievable within twenty generations under selection for tameness.

nodes.s: Round enclosures on a hillside in Anatolia holding T-shaped pillars carved to suggest human figures, built by people who had not yet domesticated a single animal - used for over a thousand years, then deliberately filled in and built over.
nodes.g: The oldest thing on this site with a claim to be about figures, and the interpretation is genuinely open, which is the point. What is not in dispute: hunter-gatherers cut limestone into anthropomorphic forms with stone and bone tools, set them upright in circles, carved them with foxes, scorpions, lions and vultures, returned to them for fourteen hundred years, and then filled the enclosures in on purpose. There is no hearth, no rubbish pit and no sign that anyone lived there - people travelled to the place. UNESCO's own nomination describes the pillars as believed to represent 'ancestors, perhaps even incipient deities', and other readings have them as totemic or protective figures. Nobody has settled it, and the carvings include a great many frightening animals: the dominant imagery is not a kind face but lions, spiders, snakes and scorpions. What this site can claim is narrow and still large: for at least a millennium, people made representations of beings, went out of their way to be near them, and eventually chose to close the place where they stood. Whether the beings were ancestors is the question this entry cannot answer, and saying so is more useful here than guessing.

src.claim: Dating, construction and the absence of settlement: the structures are among the earliest evidence worldwide for human-made megalithic buildings constructed specifically for the ritual requirements of their prehistoric population, erected between approximately 9600 and 8200 BC in the Pre-Pottery Neolithic, some 6,000 years before Stonehenge. The T-shaped pillars 'embodying a schematised anthropomorphic figure' were carved from the adjacent limestone plateau with stone and bone tools. The enclosures were probably used for public rituals, possibly of a funerary nature, and feasting.
src.citation: Göbekli Tepe (Turkey), No 1572: nomination and evaluation. UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 2018.

src.claim: The interpretive status, in the words of the nominating body, and the deliberate closure: 'The anthropomorphic T-shaped pillars are believed to be representations of ancestors, perhaps even incipient deities.' The enclosures of Layer III were then 'intentionally backfilled', the fills containing numerous animal bones 'probably the result of large feasts'.
src.citation: Executive Summary, Göbekli Tepe (Turkey), No 1572. UNESCO World Heritage Centre.

src.claim: That it was a place people travelled to rather than lived: the remains of undomesticated plant material and tens of thousands of wild animal bones - chiefly gazelle - were recovered, 'but the lack of trash pits, hearths, or other signals of domestic life indicates that it was most likely not a permanent settlement'; most experts identify it as a ritual site 'that may have attracted worshipers from great distances'. First investigated in the 1960s and dismissed as a medieval cemetery before its true age was established in the 1990s.
src.citation: Gobekli Tepe. Encyclopaedia Britannica.

src.claim: Site description and the imagery: circular enclosures each containing two large T-shaped pillars ringed by smaller stones facing inward, the tallest around 16 feet and up to 50 tons; carvings including foxes, scorpions, lions, vultures and other wild animals; site known by the Turkish name meaning 'belly hill'.
src.citation: Göbekli Tepe. Wikipedia.

nodes.s: Myths are not stories people tell once. They are stories with a fixed shape that get told to the same audience on a schedule.
nodes.g: The oldest parasocial structure there is: fixed, repeatable, known in advance, and useless for anything except the purpose it was made for. Everything after is a variant.

src.claim: The deep structure this site keeps rediscovering, from a source far older than fandom: Victor Turner's account of ritual and communitas, in which people temporarily become equal in a shared symbolic space and the intensity of that experience is the point
src.citation: Turner, V. W. (1969). The Ritual Process: Structure and Meaning.

src.claim: Campbell's monomyth is the version everyone cites and it is the least reliable part of the package - worth saying so, since the site should not smuggle a contested framework in as settled
src.citation: Campbell, J. (1949). The Hero with a Thousand Faces.

nodes.t: The craft of the sage Adapa
nodes.s: A tablet from Nineveh written in the voice of Ashurbanipal, listing what he had been taught and by whom - a named sage he never met - and then what he did with it, which was to put the tablets in his palace for the instruction of his subjects.
nodes.g: A named individual, dead or legendary, reached entirely through writing, and a resume of the arrangement. The School Days Inscription reads: I learned the craft of the sage Adapa, the secret hidden lore, all of the scribal arts; I am able to recognise celestial and terrestrial omens and can discuss them in an assembly of scholars; I have read cunningly written texts in obscure Sumerian and Akkadian that are difficult to interpret. Everything the tie required was on one side of it. The teacher never appears, and the whole apparatus existed so that what he had absorbed could be performed in a room full of other people. Then the sentence that is this site in one line: I have written upon tablets the noble products of the work of the scribe, and I have placed them in my palace for the instruction of my subjects. A clerk's counter that serves everybody, built by the only man in Assyria who could read the stock his own nobles could not. Two things keep it from being a parable. The collection was assembled partly by coercion - Babylonian scribes were taken captive during the campaigns and set to work in the royal libraries, so the archive that taught the world was built by people who did not choose to be in it. And when Nineveh fell in 612 BC the fire that destroyed the palace baked the tablets into ceramic: the destruction is the only reason the library can be read now. It survived by being destroyed, which is this site's argument about archives in one accident.

src.citation: Finkel, I., & Taylor, J. Cuneiform. The British Museum. Quoted in Missed History, The Lost Library of Ashurbanipal.
src.claim: Both quotations. The School Days Inscription, described as reading almost like a modern-day resume: I learned the craft of the sage Adapa, the secret hidden lore, all of the scribal arts; I am able to recognise celestial and terrestrial omens and can discuss them in an assembly of scholars; I have read cunningly written texts in obscure Sumerian and Akkadian that are difficult to interpret. And Ashurbanipal's statement of purpose: I have written upon tablets the noble products of the work of the scribe, and I have placed them in my palace for the instruction of my subjects.

src.citation: Ashurbanipal Library Project, A royal collection. ORACC, University of Pennsylvania Museum, with the British Museum.
src.claim: Scale and standing: a combination of dedicated scholar and supremely powerful ruler, he gathered at Nineveh an unrivalled wealth of specialist knowledge accumulated over many centuries; the largest, broadest and most important library ever assembled over 3,500 years of cuneiform culture, and until the Library of Alexandria the most significant library of antiquity, with almost 32,000 tablets and fragments surviving.

src.citation: Ashurbanipal Library Project, Assembling the Library and Library colophons. ORACC and the British Museum.
src.claim: How the collection was assembled and who was in it: tablets bear colophons naming Ashurbanipal, and around a quarter record individual scribes, most appearing only once; acquisition lists from 648 BC show many individuals donating only a tablet or a handful. Separately, that Babylonian scribes were taken captive during the campaigns and forced to work in the royal libraries.

src.citation: Library of Ashurbanipal. Wikipedia.
src.claim: The destruction as preservation: Nineveh was destroyed in 612 BCE and a great fire during the burning of the palace is believed to have baked the clay cuneiform tablets, which is why so much Mesopotamian literature survives at all.

nodes.s: Plato describes an older man in love with a boy who is compared, in the text, to a hunting animal that is deaf. The animal's ears are the point: the love is addressed to someone who cannot hear it, and the whole scene turns on that.
nodes.g: The earliest surviving description of this site's subject written down by someone who was inside the institution rather than looking at it from outside, and it is startling how modern the anatomy is. In the Phaedrus the lover hunts a beast that is 'shag-eared and deaf', and the closing image is the one nobody expects: having finally got what he chased, the lover finds himself running away and the *beast* pursuing him, because it never understood the terms. The one-sided party was not withholding. It was deaf. And in the First Alcibiades, Alcibiades tells Socrates that he is the only lover who has not abandoned the suit and that the others 'pestered you with their conversation' while he stayed silent for years - so the same structure is described from both ends, which almost nothing else on this site manages. It is also the first entry here where the power asymmetry is institutional rather than accidental, and the first where a written text tells you that role reversals were constant: the beloved could become the lover. Whether that is friendship or something else was never settled, which is why it belongs here.

src.claim: The figure, from the primary text. The Phaedrus compares the beloved to a beast 'put together anyhow; he has a short thick neck; he is flat-faced and of a dark colour, with grey eyes and blood-red complexion; the mate of insolence and pride, shag-eared and deaf, hardly yielding to whip and spur'. And the reversal: 'he changes pursuit into flight, while the other is compelled to follow him with passion and imprecation not knowing that he ought never from the first to have accepted a demented lover instead of a sensible non-lover'.
src.citation: Plato. Phaedrus. Translated by Benjamin Jowett. Internet Classics Archive.

src.claim: The other end of it, from the primary text: 'Socrates, son of Cleinias, I think it must surprise you that I, the first of all your lovers, am the only one of them who has not given up his suit and thrown you over, and whereas they have all pestered you with their conversation I have not spoken one word to you for so many years.'
src.citation: Plato. Alcibiades I, 103a. Perseus Digital Library, Tufts University.

src.claim: That role reversals were normal rather than exceptional - 'role reversals between lover and beloved are constant, as they are in the Symposium' - and that the dialogue was composed around 370 BC, alongside the Republic and the Symposium.
src.citation: Phaedrus (dialogue). Wikipedia.

src.claim: The setting that makes the entry's structural point: in the Symposium the speeches are given at Agathon's house by a company including Phaedrus, Aristophanes, Agathon, Socrates and - arriving drunk and late - Alcibiades, who insists on singing 'the praises of Socrates' in the character of 'a disappointed lover'.
src.citation: Plato. Symposium. Translated by Benjamin Jowett. Project Gutenberg, e-text 1600.

nodes.t: The wax masks in the hall
nodes.s: A Roman aristocrat had a wax mask of his own face taken while he was alive - usually in his thirties or forties, on taking office - and it was kept in a cupboard in the entrance hall beside a painted family tree and a label listing his offices. He never saw it worn. After his death, actors put it on and walked it in his funeral procession, in order of death, wearing the robes of the office he had held.
nodes.g: The best-documented one-sided attachment in this corpus, and thirteen thousand years later than the dog - which is the point. Everything here is checkable, because it was written down, and what it shows is how completely a bond can be built with someone who cannot answer. The mask never speaks: eye-holes and a gap between the lips were cut into it so that the *actor* could see and talk, and the inscription beside it did the conversing. Children grew up walking past it daily - Valerius Maximus has a man recalling that he called the dead his parents and drew his standing from their masks - and it had states: opened at festivals, hung with laurel on an election, closed during mourning. It was also an inheritance that changed address, going with a bride into her husband's house, and it was not uniformly flattering: Pliny's son was described as burdened by the masks he carried. No mask survives. All of it comes from authors.

src.claim: Technique and chronology: masks were cast from a plaster mould taken from the living face, generally between the ages of 35 and 40 and on attaining the aedileship; they were called death masks but were unquestionably made during life and only displayed after death; they were already well established by the 2nd century BC and in use into the 4th and perhaps the 6th century AD. Eyes and a strip between the lips were cut out so the actor could see and speak. No wax mask has survived and there are no ancient depictions of them, so their appearance rests entirely on literary accounts - Polybius and Pliny the Elder chiefly.
src.citation: Rose, C. B., & Lovink, M. (2014). Recreating Roman Wax Masks. Expedition Magazine, 56(3). Penn Museum. Originally published 1 December 2014.

src.claim: The documented mechanism, which is the useful part: masks were kept in armaria in the atrium beside tituli listing consulships, censorships and triumphs, and beside painted portraits linked into a stemma. Tacitus calls the funeral procession the pompa imaginum (Ann. 4.9), with actors in the masks and magisterial dress in order of death. Cicero Phil. 2.26 has the Bruti seeing the mask of Lucius Brutus daily; Val. Max. 5.5.praef has a man recalling that he called the dead his parents and drew equal glory from the masks; Pliny Ep. 3.3.6 describes a son being burdened by which masks he carried, and Ep. 8.10.3 hopes to leave children 'non subitas imagines' - not new masks. The armaria were opened at festivals, hung with laurel on electoral success and closed in mourning. Copies of a bride's imagines passed into her husband's house (Cic. Vat. 28; Senatus Consultum de Cn. Pisone patre 76-82, 20 CE). The right to hold imagines was customary rather than statutory.
src.citation: Webb, L. (2023). Gendering the Roman imago. Eugesta, 7(2017). DOI: 10.54563/eugesta.550

nodes.t: Eight thousand faces, all facing outward
nodes.s: Eight thousand life-size soldiers, each with a face and ears no other has, buried in battle order facing the enemy with the emperor behind them - made from the likenesses of real men so the substitute army would stand where the real one could not.
nodes.g: This site's structure with the arrow turned round. Everywhere else here, one person attaches to another who cannot answer. Here eight thousand specific likenesses were manufactured so that a single man would never be without an army, and every figure faces away from him. The 2022 analysis in npj Heritage Science found the features highly resemble those of contemporary Chinese people and concluded the figures were crafted from real portraits and intended to constitute a real army to protect the emperor in the afterlife, as if he was alive, the artificial army being the substitution of his real one. A substituted army of individuals, each one somebody, each one distinct enough to be identified by ear. That is more intimate than anything the twentieth century built and nobody chose it. The cost belongs in the entry rather than in a footnote to it: young women of the court were buried with him, some apparently dismembered and laid outside the passageways, and reconstructions have since been made of two of their faces. An entry about eight thousand distinct faces should not be allowed to be charming.

src.citation: Measurement and analysis of facial features of terracotta warriors based on high-precision 3D point clouds. npj Heritage Science, 10, 2022. DOI: 10.1038/s40494-022-00662-0
src.claim: The finding the entry rests on: facial features highly resemble those of contemporary Chinese people, indicating that the figures were crafted from real portraits and intended to constitute a real army to protect the emperor in the afterlife, as if he was alive, the constructed army being more likely the substitution of his real army. Quantitative 3D point-cloud and anthropometric work found the scatter of measured features random, no two identical, each figure having distinct features which seem like real humans. Notes that it was still debated whether the figures were based on individual people or standardised models.

src.citation: Qin Mausoleum and Terra Cotta Army. Exploring Chinese History: Culture, Archaeology, ibiblio.
src.claim: Number, disposition and intention: 8,099 life-size figures of warriors and horses, buried with the first emperor in 210-209 BCE; all 8,099 soldiers are unique and distinguishable with different height and facial features; each figure's head appears to be unique, showing a variety of facial features, expressions and hair styles. The army was built facing enemy territory, between those enemies and the emperor's tomb, and was created in the belief that it would protect him after his death.

src.citation: Chen, S. (2018, July 13). Could these be the faces of the murdered wife and son of China's first emperor Qin Shi Huang? South China Morning Post.
src.claim: The cost the entry carries: young women from the emperor's court who had not borne children were buried with him, some historians believing they were buried alive; the dismembered body of a woman of about twenty was found among around a hundred tombs, with bodies dismembered and placed outside passageways leading to the burial chambers. Chinese researchers have since reconstructed the faces of a young woman and a young man from these tombs. Publisher returns 403 to an unauthenticated request.

nodes.s: A regular assembled audience for a figure who addresses them, in a building, on a schedule, for years.
nodes.g: The largest organised parasocial arrangement in history, and the one the field has never taken seriously as one. It has a leader, a schedule, a building, an emotional register, an exegesis tradition and a revenue model.

src.claim: A fan forum is a functioning community, not a comment box: K-pop stan Twitter operates as a Community of Practice - members form interpersonal bonds, communicate regularly, and contribute in their own capacities
src.citation: Malik, Z., & Haidar, S. (2020). Online community development through social interaction - K-Pop stan twitter as a community of practice. Interactive Learning Environments, 31(2).

src.claim: AND THE FINDING NOBODY NOTICES: that community has a power hierarchy among its participants - described by the authors as 'usually the least noticed aspect in research on online platforms'. The folklore of equal fans is empirically false
src.citation: Malik, Z., & Haidar, S. (2020). Interactive Learning Environments, 31(2).

src.claim: Why the congregation forms: PSRs develop because they fulfil a need to belong and are maintained through parasocial interaction and fandom activity; the authors conclude they may need redefining because fans perceive reciprocity. N=126 stan / N=111 non-stan / N=12 interviews
src.citation: Y/N and OOMFs: Development, Maintenance, and Consequences of Parasocial Relationships on Stan Twitter (2024). Asia Social Issues.

src.claim: The congregation is not a consolation prize. Some fans attributed the friends they most wanted to be close with to their fanship itself
src.citation: Ascue et al., Annyeong, Saranghae: A Phenomenological Study on the Effects of Parasocial Relationships between Adult Filipino K-pop Fans and their Idols. De La Salle University.

src.claim: Scale and intensity: 63% of adolescent fans (14-18) agreed or strongly agreed with at least 10 of 20 parasocial interaction scale items, 13% strongly agreed with 15 or more, and 52% reported over two hours a day on their idol's content
src.citation: The Psychological Impact of Parasocial Relationships on Adolescent K-pop Fans (explanatory sequential mixed methods, Ontario).

src.claim: The verdict, in the participants' own words: 'You feel as if you've known them for a long time' - said about an idol sharing his feelings on a livestream
src.citation: Ascue et al., Annyeong, Saranghae (De La Salle University).

nodes.s: The sculptor who fell in love with his own work. The statue was never going to be able to leave, and the story treats that as part of the appeal rather than a tragedy to be corrected.
nodes.g: Not the origin - the archaeology in this file runs tens of thousands of years further back, and Roman wax imagines predate Ovid by two and a half centuries. What this is: the first time the structure was written down deliberately, by a Roman, as a story worth telling about a man who loved something that could not leave. The telling detail was never that he loved a statue. It was that the statue was never going to be able to leave, and that this seems to have been part of the appeal. The feeling is real and entirely structured around the other party's inability to reciprocate, and everyone since has rediscovered it.

src.claim: the entry as a whole
src.citation: Ovid. Metamorphoses, Book X. Published ca. AD 8; Ovid 43 BC - 17/18 AD.

nodes.s: A person who hears the specifics, performs the ritual, and knows the family history, on a repeating cycle.
nodes.g: The most complete parasocial arrangement available and it includes a uniform, a script and a confession. It is also the arrangement the most people are inside of, which is the strongest evidence that the form is universal rather than a symptom.

src.claim: THE ENTIRE ARGUMENT OF THIS SITE, IN ONE ABSTRACT. Followers turn to priests' social posts for scriptural insight and a sense of connection, yet their engagement rarely extends beyond viewing, liking, sharing and brief thanks. Priests seldom reply, solicit topics, or host real-time dialogue. N=20
src.citation: Between pulpit and platform: Parasocial bonds in Filipino priests' social media ministry (2025). Taylor's FSLM Journals.

src.claim: And the finding that indicts the apparatus: the ties REMAIN parasocial - one-sided and deferential - EVEN AS priests adopt influencer cues such as eye-catching thumbnails, follower milestones and donation links. Identical equipment, reciprocity that never arrives
src.citation: Between pulpit and platform (2025).

src.claim: Cultivation and harvesting, named as such by someone studying it as evangelism: seven pastors using YouTube, Facebook, Instagram and TikTok use the same techniques as secular influencers to cultivate PSRs - frequent posting, direct address, self-disclosure, consistent authenticity
src.citation: Witzel, L. D. The Cultivation and Harvesting of Parasocial Relationships for Evangelism: An Exploratory Multiple Case Study of Pastors' Use of Video on Social Media (Liberty University doctoral dissertation).

src.claim: And the one technique conspicuously MISSING: expressing positive feelings. The emotional register the secular apparatus requires most is the one the priests dropped, and the harvest step changed accordingly - secular influencers monetize, priests direct people into a spiritual journey
src.citation: Witzel, The Cultivation and Harvesting of Parasocial Relationships for Evangelism.

src.claim: The field's own velocity, for scale: papers on parasocial experience grew fourfold between 2013 and 2020, with over 400 peer-reviewed papers and dissertations published in 2024 alone
src.citation: Witzel, citing Liebers & Schramm (2023) and Forster, The Oxford Handbook of Parasocial Experiences (2023).

nodes.s: Walrus-ivory chess pieces from around 1150, buried on the Isle of Lewis and dug up in 1831, now divided between two museums and at least four incomplete sets. Two of them are probably replacements made in another workshop to replace pieces that had been lost.
nodes.g: The one case on this site where the attachment and its object are both fully documented, from twelfth-century Norway to a museum curator writing in 2012. James Robinson, curator of Late Medieval Collections at the British Museum, on how people meet them: they visit the museum and are 'completely transfixed', and 'instinctively naming one of them "Noggin"' - he and Irving Finkel did exactly that. The name then travelled further than the object: the animator Peter Firmin drew Noggin with his queen, and a manga artist built two exhibitions and a publication with the museum out of them. What makes it sharper than a curiosity is that these are carved mythological types rather than portraits - several are read as berserkers from Snorri's Heimskringla - and that the hoard comprises at least four incomplete sets with two pieces probably made in a different workshop to replace lost ones. So the figures people have named and bonded with for two centuries include at least two replacements, and no visitor can tell which. A counter clerk who cannot remember you, carved in ivory, and shipped in pieces.

src.claim: The object and its disassembly: 12th-century walrus ivory and whales' teeth, discovered 1831 on the Isle of Lewis; the hoard contained 94 objects - 78 chess pieces, 14 tablemen and a belt buckle - of which 82 pieces are owned by the British Museum and 11 by the National Museum of Scotland; the pieces come from at least four distinct but incomplete sets, nine cannot be assigned to any group, and 'it is not clear if a single complete period-accurate set can be assembled from the pieces'. Some pieces bore traces of red stain, indicating red and white were used to distinguish the two sides rather than the modern black and white. All the pieces in the back rank are sculptures of human figures.
src.citation: Lewis chessmen. Wikipedia.

src.claim: The two replacement pieces - a king and a warder - which 'may have been made at a different workshop entirely, perhaps to replace missing or broken pieces'.
src.citation: Lewis chessmen. Wikipedia, citing National Museums Scotland.

They, like Irving Finkel, visited the museum and were completely transfixed by the chessmen, instinctively naming one of them "Noggin."' The name then propagated: Peter Firmin drew Noggin with his queen, and Hoshino Yukinobu collaborated with the British Museum on two exhibitions and a publication. Also the character-level detail: 'a delightful sculpture in miniature, with a specific, individualized character' - kings sitting with swords on their laps, some long-haired and bearded and others clean shaven, knights with distinct headgear, different shields and different shaggy ponies.

nodes.s: English woman who experienced what she described as an unbreakable bond with Jesus, was mocked for weeping in church, was reviled by her family, and in 1438 dictated a book about it that persuaded other women to do the same.
nodes.g: The single strongest real case in the catalogue, and it is eight hundred years early. A bond with a figure who never appears in the physical world. A text as the medium. Grief when the access was withdrawn, which is the Replika update. And a recruitment function: the book exists to make other women feel what she felt, which is what a parasocial relationship is for.

src.claim: Kempe dictated The Book of My First Showings c.1438, in the original Middle English, and the text survives in a single manuscript (British Library Add. 39903). She dictated it to scribes because she could not write.
src.citation: Kempe, Margaret (ed. Frances E. Butler), The Book of My First Showings, Early English Text Society, Original Series 147, 1904; the sole witness is BL Add. 39903, transcribed in the 1904 EETS edition.

src.claim: She was imprisoned in 1415-1416 largely over this writing and its reception.
src.citation: Kempe's later accounts name imprisonment by the Bishop of London; the 1438 text is conventionally read against it.

nodes.s: Performing a self until the self holds, where it can be witnessed. Margery Kempe in white clothes in a world where widows wore black, weeping loudly in public for years, having decided she was going to be a specific kind of person.
nodes.g: The founding document. It has three ingredients - a public, a performance, and witnesses who disapprove - and every parasocial dynamic since has those three. The neighbours thought she was unwell. The only thing that has changed is what the audience thinks about the person who is unwell.

src.claim: the entry as a whole
src.citation: Kempe, M. The Book of Margery Kempe

nodes.t: The Book of My First Showings
nodes.s: A short prose book dictated by Margery Kempe describing her experiences of Christ's love, her suffering, and her certainty that she had been chosen.
nodes.g: The first person in this catalogue to write the thing down and then hand the book to other people. That second half is the part that makes it parasocial rather than merely devotional: the text is an instrument for producing the bond in somebody else.

src.claim: Composed c.1438, surviving in one manuscript.
src.citation: See the EETS edition cited under margery-kempe.

nodes.s: Author of Don Quixote, and of a narrator who keeps having to explain away the reality of what his character is doing.
nodes.g: Wrote the book in which the gap between a fictional world and a real one is argued out loud, by the person best placed to know.

src.claim: Author; the two parts were published 1605 and 1615.
src.citation: Standard bibliographic record.

nodes.s: A room of people responding to a performance, learning the timing of the person on the stage.
nodes.g: Theatre invented the responsestream, and the performer learns to read it. Two thousand years before a chat log, the same feedback loop with worse latency and a room.

nodes.s: An old man who reads so many books about chivalry that he goes out to live as a knight, against all evidence.
nodes.g: The founding case of a reader who mistakes a book for a world and then lives in it anyway. The whole book's plot is the argument that a person can be entirely sincere about a bond with something that is not there, and the reader is not asked to think less of him for it.

src.claim: Cervantes, Don Quixote, part one 1605, part two 1615.
src.citation: Cervantes Saavedra, Miguel de, Don Quixote, 1605 and 1615.

nodes.g: Wrote the most influential suicide in European literature and then spent his life doing the opposite of his character.

src.citation: Standard biographical record.

nodes.t: The wall exists to keep you out
nodes.s: Diderot invented the wall in 1758 for the purpose of stopping the audience noticing. Every breach since - a wink, a clap, a lecture - is that convention failing on purpose, and it is the only time the far side admits you are there.
nodes.g: The convention is an engineering specification for invisibility, and this entire site is about what happens on the far side of it. Diderot put it exactly where it belongs in 1758: actors and writers should "imagine a huge wall across the front of the stage, separating you from the audience, and behave exactly as if the curtain had never risen". The wall is not a description of the stage. It is a condition of it, and the condition is that you are not supposed to know. What happened to the phrase afterwards is the small, exact history of the idea. Diderot's *un grand mur* became **the fourth wall** to Leigh Hunt in 1807, writing about the actor Mr. Bannister: "No actor enters so well into the spirit of his audience as well as his author, for he engages your attention immediately by seeming to care nothing about you; the stage appears to be his own room, of which the audience compose the fourth wall." Henry Irving wrote in February 1879 that "the stage has four walls, though the fourth is only theoretical", and the first known use of **fourth wall theory** follows later that month in a comment on that article in the British periodical *Truth*. Vincent Canby called it "that invisible scrim that forever separates the audience from the stage" in 1987. Two hundred and forty years to get from a wall that keeps you out to a scrim that does the same job more honestly. Breaking it matters here because it is the **only** moment the figure admits that an audience exists - and the strongest version is not a wink. In *Peter Pan* the breach is an instruction the audience obeys: "If you believe in fairies, clap your hands!" said to revive Tinker Bell, who lives or dies according to whether strangers in the dark choose to believe. That is the parasocial condition with the volume turned up, because the fiction's survival is now a real person's decision rather than a fiction's. Bugs Bunny and the Warner Bros. characters broke it regularly, per the reference, in shorts like *Daffy Duck and Egghead* (1938) and *Thugs with Dirty Mugs* (1939) - which is the rabbit that talks to the audience, and he is documented, unlike anything called Harvey. **Two honesty notes, and the second is the reason this is an entry and not a sub-category.** First, in mockumentary the camera may be *inside* the fiction, so looking into it is not a breach at all - a convention only counts if the audience knows it is one. Second, and this is the boundary the whole site turns on: **a fictional figure acknowledging that an audience exists is not a real person acknowledging you.** Deadpool looks at the lens and cannot hear you. A streamer reads your comment aloud and the far side can hear you, which is what `transparasocial` means here. Same gesture, opposite structure, and a taxonomy that could not tell them apart would be a taxonomy that could not classify the thing it exists to classify.

src.citation: Fourth wall. Wikipedia.
src.claim: The definition and the whole etymology: 'Breaking the fourth wall in a narrative, particularly in drama, is the action of characters violating the convention of the fourth wall, for instance when performers in a play speak directly to or even interact with the audience, when movie or television characters speak directly into the camera, when protagonists in a novel acknowledge the artificiality of the story they are in, or generally whenever fictional characters openly refer to themselves as such.' The concept 'is often attributed to philosopher, critic and dramatist Denis Diderot, who wrote in 1758 that actors and writers should "imagine a huge wall across the front of the stage, separating you from the audience, and behave exactly as if the curtain had never risen"'. Diderot's 'un grand mur' 'became "the fourth wall" to Leigh Hunt when in 1807 referring to Mr. Bannister': 'No actor enters so well into the spirit of his audience as well as his author, for he engages your attention immediately by seeming to care nothing about you; the stage appears to be his own room, of which the audience compose the fourth wall.' Henry Irving, February 1879: 'It should never be forgotten that the stage has four walls, though the fourth is only theoretical.' 'The first known use of "fourth wall theory" follows later that month in a comment on that article in the British periodical Truth.' Vincent Canby 1987: 'that invisible scrim that forever separates the audience from the stage.' Also: 'Breaking the fourth wall is especially common in pantomime and children's theater where - for example, a character might ask the children for help, as when Peter Pan appeals to the audience to applaud in an effort to revive the fading Tinker Bell ("If you believe in fairies, clap your hands!")'. Cinema: Mary MacLane's 1918 Men Who Have Made Love to Me, 'the enigmatic author - who portrays herself - interrupts the vignettes onscreen to address the audience directly'; Reefer Madness (1936), Josef Forte as Dr. Alfred Carroll; Groucho Marx in Animal Crackers (1930) and Horse Feathers (1932), the latter advising viewers to 'go out to the lobby'; 'Characters in theatrical animated cartoons, particularly Bugs Bunny and other characters in Warner Bros.' Looney Tunes and Merrie Melodies shorts, regularly broke the fourth wall', with Tex Avery's Daffy Duck and Egghead (1938) and Thugs with Dirty Mugs (1939) named. Woody Allen on Annie Hall (1977): 'I felt many of the people in the audience had the same feelings and the same problems. I wanted to talk to them directly and confront them.' Jerry Lewis, The Total Filmmaker (1971): 'Some film-makers believe you should never have an actor look directly into the camera... I think that is nonsense, and usually I have my actors, in a single, look direct into the camera at least once in a film, if a point is to be served.' And the mockumentary exemption, which is the important one: 'because the camera crew and interview situation may be part of the fictional documentary frame, looking at or speaking to the camera does not always function as a convention.'

nodes.s: The young man of Goethe's novel who reads too much, loves a woman who does not love him back, and kills himself, in a book that made that behaviour fashionable across Europe for a decade.
nodes.g: The prototype of the reader who goes looking for a character in order to feel something, and then brings the feeling home. Published in 1774; within two years the resulting condition had a name, Wertherfieber, and ministers of religion were issuing warnings about it.

src.claim: Goethe, The Sorrows of Young Werther, 1774; the Werther fever it provoked is documented in the reception history of the period.
src.citation: Goethe, J. W. von, Die Leiden des jungen Werthers, 1774; reception documented in the standard accounts of European sensibility.

nodes.s: Serialised fiction to a mass audience, weekly, to people who could not afford a book but could not afford not to read it.
nodes.g: Built the first audience for fiction that was reliably weekly, enormous, and not present in the room.

src.claim: Novelist and serial publisher; dates standard.
src.citation: Standard biographical record.

nodes.s: A woman in Great Expectations who is left jilted at the altar, stops eating, ages, and arranges to be found the way she was on her wedding day - decades later, in a wedding dress, in a darkened room.
nodes.g: The most complete fictional treatment of the object of a parasocial bond being a person who was never real, and of the grief outliving the reasons for it. She is not a metaphor for a fictional character, she is a person who has mistaken her own wedding for a plot.

src.claim: Dickens, Great Expectations, 1861, Book 1, chapter 8 and chapter 19.
src.citation: Dickens, Charles, Great Expectations, 1861.

nodes.s: Supporting a club as a condition of belonging to a place, a class, a family, or a city.
nodes.g: A parasocial bond with an address. The team is the only large-scale attachment in modern life that arrives with geography attached, which is why a relegation is felt as a personal event by people who have never met the players.

src.claim: The mechanism, fifty years before anyone wrote about parasocial relationships: identification with a group is itself a source of self-esteem, and people derive it from membership rather than from any property of the team
src.citation: Tajfel, H., & Turner, J. C. (1979). An integrative theory of intergroup conflict.

nodes.s: A loyalty scheme by paper coupon, redeemable at any participating shop, popular decades before loyalty cards existed.
nodes.g: The first loyalty scheme, and it is already the whole modern mechanism: a discount in exchange for the customer choosing this shop repeatedly. The paper only changed.

src.claim: A peer-reviewed history of the mechanism in the United States, covering 1891-2008. The title's own span is what dates the entry: the documented run of trading stamps begins in 1891, not the decade earlier this entry previously claimed.
src.citation: Elnahla, N., & Neilson, L. C. Getting something for nothing: the history of trading stamps in the United States of America (1891-2008).

src.claim: Schuster's Department Store, Milwaukee issued the first stamps in 1890-91, specifically to push cash customers away from credit; L.H. Parke followed in 1895; S&H Green Stamps launched 1896, first customer a housewife in a Jackson, Michigan dry goods store
src.citation: Something for everyone? The rise and fall of trading stamps (2024), drawing on the Hartman Center archives, Duke University.

src.citation: Trading Stamps. Encyclopedia.com.

src.citation: Johnson, C. K. Trading stamps and the retailer. (USDA Marketing Division studies).

src.citation: Ascue et al., Annyeong, Saranghae (De La Salle University).

nodes.s: The painter stands in front of the figure he made and asks whether the man is really like it. He is. And it will never alter, which is the only thing about it anybody wanted.
nodes.g: The purest statement of the mirrored case ever written, and it is four lines of dialogue rather than an argument. Basil Hallward has painted the man he loves and the painting will not age, and when the original walks over to the canvas and asks the only question that matters - 'Am I really like that?' - the painter answers 'Yes; you are just like that' and then, 'At least you are like it in appearance. But it will never alter.' The real man is standing right there. He is also the wrong one. Wilde's book is about a portrait that takes the ruin instead, and the two sentences above are why anybody wants it: every bond on this site wants the other end to be permanent, and here is a version where permanence is available and it is attached to the wrong object. Dorian's own side of it is the jealousy that names the mechanism exactly - 'I am jealous of everything whose beauty does not die. I am jealous of the portrait you have painted of me. Why should it keep what I must lose? Every moment that passes takes something from me and gives something to it.' He wants to be the copy. The most damning detail is a mirror. Having seen the cruelty in the painted mouth, he takes up a glass and looks at his own red lips to check, and they are fine: 'No line like that warped his red lips.' The mirror is the one witness that could have settled it and it exonerates him. He is not permitted to be the evidence about himself. That is what the third axis calls mirrored - the figure supplied by the person attached to it, edited toward what the attachment needs, with the original never consulted - and Wilde wrote it in 1890, a hundred and thirty years before anybody had a word for it. First published in the July 1890 issue of Lippincott's Monthly Magazine, the only novel Wilde ever wrote.

src.citation: Wilde, O. The Picture of Dorian Gray. Project Gutenberg eBook 174 (full text).
src.claim: The dialogue, quoted exactly from the full text. Hallward: 'I shall stay with the real Dorian,' he said, sadly. 'Is it the real Dorian?' cried the original of the portrait, strolling across to him. 'Am I really like that?' 'Yes; you are just like that.' 'How wonderful, Basil!' 'At least you are like it in appearance. But it will never alter,' sighed Hallward. 'That is something.' Dorian: 'I am jealous of everything whose beauty does not die. I am jealous of the portrait you have painted of me. Why should it keep what I must lose? Every moment that passes takes something from me and gives something to it. Oh, if it were only the other way! If the picture could change, and I could be always what I am now!' And the mirror, in the same book: 'the lines of cruelty round the mouth as clearly as if he had been looking into a mirror after he had done some dreadful thing. He winced and, taking up from the table an oval glass framed in ivory Cupids, one of Lord Henry's many presents to him, glanced hurriedly into its polished depths. No line like that warped his red lips.'

src.citation: The Picture of Dorian Gray. Wikipedia.
src.claim: Publication history: an 1890 philosophical fiction and Gothic horror novel by Oscar Wilde; a shorter novella-length version was published in the July 1890 issue of Lippincott's Monthly Magazine, the novel-length version in April 1891. It is the only novel Wilde wrote. The story concerns a portrait of Dorian Gray painted by Basil Hallward, 'a friend of Dorian's and an artist infatuated with Dorian's beauty' - the description is the bond, stated by the encyclopedia's own lead.

nodes.s: A recurring cast of characters, in a fixed panel order, appearing every single day without exception for decades.
nodes.g: The first daily serial in print and the template for the daily TV schedule that followed it. Continuity is the mechanism: you come back because yesterday happened to them too.

src.claim: The newspaper strip was the first mass parasocial apparatus: a recurring, scheduled, addressed-to-everyone relationship delivered daily to a reader who never had to identify themselves to receive it
src.citation: Comic strip (Wikipedia).

nodes.s: Director who said he made films about the tension between a man and the thing he cannot have.
nodes.g: Stated the thesis of this whole site, in his own words, before the word parasocial existed.

src.claim: Statements in interview about suspense being the withholding of information, and about Vertigo's protagonist.
src.citation: Hitchcock on Hitchcock, ed. François Truffaut, 1966 - the Vertigo chapter covers this directly.

nodes.s: An adult with authority over a child for years, who is remembered partly by how they made them feel at nine.
nodes.g: A bond that shapes adult attachment patterns decades later, entirely outside anything the parasocial literature studies. Most people's template for one-sided attachment is a coach and they have never been asked about it.

src.citation: Holt, N. L., Neely, K. C., Slater, L. G., Camire, M., Cote, J., Fraser-Thomas, J., MacDonald, D., Strachan, L., & Tamminen, K. A. (2017). A grounded theory of positive youth development through sport based on results from a qualitative meta-study. International Review of Sport and Exercise Psychology, 10(1), 1-49. (First published online 4 September 2016.)
src.claim: A meta-synthesis of 63 qualitative studies, and the direct refutation of this entry's claim that nobody has asked about the coach. One of its three emergent categories is the 'PYD climate' - adult relationships, peer relationships and parental involvement. It reports that 'positive and sustained adult-youth relations' is one of the Big 3 programme characteristics associated with development; that Cote, Turnidge & Evans' Personal Assets Framework places 'relational factors (i.e., quality relationships)' among its three elements, generating change in confidence, competence, connection and character when repeated over time; and that Catalano et al. list 'warm, supportive relationships' among eight programme characteristics. Open access, CC BY-NC-ND.

src.citation: Cote, J., & Gilbert, W. (2009). An Integrative Definition of Coaching Effectiveness and Expertise. International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching, 4(3), 307-323.
src.claim: The source of the 4 Cs that coaching effectiveness is measured against: competence, confidence, connection and character. Connection is defined as 'positive bonds and social relationships with people inside and outside of sport' - so the relational bond is one of the four things a coach is explicitly judged on producing. Volume and issue confirmed against Crossref as 4(3); the journal's own landing page says 4(4), and Crossref was preferred. Publisher returns 403 to an unauthenticated request.

nodes.s: A named individual with access to your home, your deposits and your address, met in person, repeatedly, under stress.
nodes.g: A parasocial relationship with somebody who holds a key and a legal claim. Section 07 exists because the feeling and the power are inversely related, which is the definition of the problem.

src.citation: Byrne, M., & McArdle, R. (2020). Secure occupancy, power and the landlord-tenant relation: a qualitative exploration of the Irish private rental sector. Housing Studies, 37(1), 124-142.
src.claim: States the relationship in the terms this entry has been arguing for: tenant and landlord are 'not merely equal parties to a contract, nor are they atomised market actors. They are tied together in a relationship which is both a social relationship and a power relationship' (quoted at p. 139 in McKee & Harris below). A social relationship and a power relationship in the same clause is the whole problem, and it is in the abstract of record for the subject. Publisher returns 403 to an unauthenticated request; volume, issue and pages confirmed against Crossref.

src.citation: McKee, K., & Harris, J. (2023). The role of landlords in shaping private renters' uneven experiences of home: towards a relational approach. International Journal of Housing Policy, 25(1), 101-118.
src.claim: Documents the mechanism this entry asserts. Renter interviews: tenants praised landlords who communicated well and were responsive, and yet, on further probing, 'some tenants simply did not want to raise legitimate issues or escalate complaints where issues remained unaddressed because of the risk of damaging the relationship with their landlord' - which the authors note persisted even where the relationship was described positively. The 'imagined alternative' of a negative relationship in the next tenancy was the powerful driver for accepting the status quo. A tenant staying silent to protect a relationship with someone who holds the keys and the deposit is a one-sided attachment, described here entirely in the language of housing policy. Publisher returns 403.

src.citation: Soaita, A. M. (2024). The social vibe of the tenant/landlord relationship in a 'tenant market': the case of Romania. Housing Studies, 40(11), 2428-2449.
src.claim: Frames the gap this entry sits in: while interest in private rental housing has grown, 'few studies have addressed the tenant/landlord relationship as lived' - as a relationship rather than a contract. Examines narratives of risk and the repertoires of risk mitigation that renters build. Publisher returns 403; bibliographic record confirmed against Crossref.

nodes.s: An authority figure seen daily, for years, who knows your name, your mood and your home situation.
nodes.g: The parasocial bond nobody writes about because the power is unequal and the field has spent fifty years on the unequal-power case while leaving this one alone.

src.claim: Measured in a classroom, n=248 junior high students: parasocial interaction with an instructor has a SIGNIFICANT POSITIVE impact on motivational interest (beta=.624, p<.005), which in turn reduces extraneous cognitive load
src.citation: Liu, X., & Li, C. (2024). The Effects of Social Cues in Self-Produced Micro Video Lectures on Parasocial Interaction, Motivational Interest, Extraneous Cognitive Load, and Concept Learning Performance.

src.claim: And the honest null in the same paper: adding MORE types of social cue made no measurable difference across four groups. Warmth is not a dial you can simply turn up

A second honest null, from educational YouTube: no correlation between parasocial interaction and actual LEARNING GROWTH, though a slight correlation with motivation, stronger for female participants. The bond changes how hard people try, not what they retain
src.citation: Beautemps, J., & Bresges, A. (2022). The influence of the parasocial relationship on the learning motivation and learning growth with educational YouTube videos in self regulated learning.

nodes.s: A player who has been attached to for years leaves, and the grievance is felt as betrayal by the entire locality.
nodes.g: The standard parasocial grievance story, and the one nobody frames as parasocial. The word for the feeling is betrayal, which is a relationship word, applied to a person who never signed anything.

src.citation: Merten, S., Reuland, N., Winand, M., & Marlier, M. (2020). Fan identification in football: professional football players and clubs competing for fan loyalty. Sport, Business and Management: An International Journal, 14(2), 169-187.
src.claim: The mechanism, and it runs opposite to the usual account. Measured with a fan identification scale: fans identify MORE strongly with their favourite team than with their favourite individual player, and connection to a player is weaker if he never played for that team. Identification therefore transfers between team and player and remains 'long-lasting, even after the combination of both actors has been dissolved' - compared in the paper to research on supporters of relocated clubs. So the grievance lands on the departing individual because the durable attachment is to the club. Publisher returns 403; Crossref-confirmed.

src.citation: Herd, K. (2023). Transfer patterns in the Swedish football clubs - a gift economy of loyalties and emotions. Soccer & Society, 25(3), 257-271.
src.claim: Interview study in which players and fans treat a transfer as simultaneously an investment, a step in a career and 'a pledge to supporters' - players describing real obligations and expectations of supporters, and supporters describing attachment to players. The pledge is understood as binding by both sides and documented in no contract, which is what makes the word 'betrayal' available. Concludes that the market may be described as an emotional economy in which money is a means rather than a goal. Publisher returns 403.

src.citation: Kaden, M., Brandt, C., Bauers, S. B., Bunar, J., & Hovemann, G. (2023). "I don't watch that anymore": an analysis of online comments by German soccer fans on their relationship to their favored clubs. Frontiers in Psychology, 14.
src.claim: The other side of the same bond: supporters' exits, analysed through Hirschman's exit-voice-loyalty framework. Finds German soccer fans inclined to voice rather than exit, but with demonstrable limits - some supporting a non-league club instead - and quotes the finding that consumption of professional soccer 'cannot be ceased altogether'. Notes the commercialisation critique that players are transferred 'like assets' without regard to the local fan community, producing alienation between players and fans. Open access.

src.citation: Fillis, I., & Mackay, C. (2014). Moving beyond fan typologies: the impact of social integration on team loyalty in football. Journal of Marketing Management, 30(3-4), 334-363.
src.claim: Moves past tiered fan typologies to argue that devotion is best explained through social integration and a religious frame - religiosity and sacred consumption accounting for committed supporters of a single club, who see themselves as members of it and are unlikely to transfer allegiance. Case study of a Scottish club and its supporters. Author accepted manuscript in the University of Stirling repository.

nodes.s: Episodes released in instalments, each ending unresolved, the audience expected to return for the next one.
nodes.g: The cliffhanger as an industrial practice rather than a narrative trick, and the direct ancestor of the soap and the serialised novel.

nodes.s: A national loyalty scheme in Britain, redeemed for goods, with a book of stamps kept in the house.
nodes.g: The first loyalty programme most families would have lived with for a generation, and a physical object in the home. The customer's book of stamps is an account balance that lives in a cupboard, which is a genius piece of interface design that nobody has beaten.

src.claim: Launched in the United Kingdom in 1958, Green Shield Stamps is among the longest-running trading-stamp loyalty schemes and remains in circulation decades later. The card outlived most of the shops that issued it
src.citation: Green Shield Stamps (Wikipedia).

nodes.s: A physical object that had to be opened, a volume small enough for one person to hold, and a reply that was an exception. Clara Bow, Shirley Temple, Judy Garland, all had staff whose job was correspondence. Some of it came back.
nodes.g: The relationship before the technology that supposedly caused it. What the mail got right is rhythm and scarcity: it arrived, it was opened, sometimes it was answered. What the internet removed was the reply and the rhythm, not the feeling. Every 'the internet invented parasocial relationships' argument collapses here.

src.claim: the entry as a whole
src.citation: No single source identified yet; this entry needs its sources added.

nodes.s: Support for a team or an athlete as a bond with a person, a place and a lineage, frequently inherited from a parent.
nodes.g: The most durable parasocial bond in the world and the one least discussed as parasocial, because it is assumed to be about sport. The transfer window is the standard betrayal story, which is a parasocial grievance wearing a football shirt.

src.claim: 'Fan' entered English usage for baseball spectators in the eighteenth century - the athlete-and-city bond predates the film star by a century
src.citation: Fan Culture. EBSCO Research Starters, Social Sciences and Humanities.

nodes.s: The first documented fan clubs, organised around sheet music and radio rather than film. Following became joining.
nodes.g: The behaviour did not arrive with any technology. It arrived with the possibility of being heard, and a great deal of organisation, done unpaid, by people who were young.

nodes.s: End the episode before the answer. Give the viewer a fixed slot, a daily rhythm, and a question with no resolution, and they will come back tomorrow at the same time for years.
nodes.g: The oldest engagement mechanic in media and the most efficient. A cliffhanger is not a plot device, it is a scheduling device - it converts a feeling into a diary entry. A twelve-part serial is not a story, it is a habit with characters in it.

src.claim: The scholarly account of seriality as structure rather than trick: Mittell's complex TV argues the modern serial builds meaning through accumulated paratext, discussion and anticipation across time rather than within the episode
src.citation: Mittell, J. (2015). Complex TV: The Poetics of Contemporary Television Storytelling.

src.claim: And the experimental result: 44 children assigned to serial or episodic delivery of the same story engaged more persistently with the serial
src.citation: To Pause With a Cliffhanger or a Temporary Closure: Serial vs. episodic narratives and sustained engagement.

nodes.s: Broadcast drama on a fixed daily slot, written for an audience with nowhere else to be at that hour.
nodes.g: The audience and the medium are the same thing. A radio serial is a routine, and the routine is the relationship.

src.claim: Fan mail as perceived interactivity in the 1920s-30s: listeners experienced two-way communication through letters even though radio had no interactive technology. The conclusion - that interactivity may depend on media content rather than media technology - is this site's thesis, in 2009
src.citation: Simmons, C. (2009). Dear Radio Broadcaster: Fan Mail as a Form of Perceived Interactivity.

src.claim: The finding that fans negotiated and policed their own codes of behaviour in fan magazines - a community regulating itself without a platform
src.citation: Lanckman, L. (2020). Fans, community, and conflict in the pages of 'Picture Play'. Transformative Works and Culture.

nodes.t: A magazine that did not exist
nodes.s: Street & Smith hired two men to sell a magazine on the radio. They invented a voice instead, and the listeners went asking newsdealers for the magazine that voice implied.
nodes.g: The best-documented case in this corpus of a one-sided bond producing demand for a physical object that was never manufactured, and it is the origin of the shadow as a mass medium. Street & Smith wanted to sell Detective Story Magazine, so they hired David Chrisman of an advertising agency and the writer-director William Sweets to turn the stories into a serial. Their actual plan was modest: a mysterious storyteller with a sinister voice, and then they needed a name for him. One scriptwriter, Harry Engman Charlot, proposed The Shadow. First broadcast 31 July 1930 as the narrator of the Detective Story Hour, voiced at first by James LaCurto and, four months later, by Frank Readick Jr. The stories were unrelated to the voice, and that turned out to be the whole business. Listeners found the announcer far more compelling than the fiction he was attached to, and began asking newsdealers for 'that Shadow detective magazine, even though it did not exist.' A bond with a voice generated a market for a book series that Street & Smith had to then commission, and the character's own power set is built around the axis this site is about: in radio and film he can turn himself invisible - except for his shadow, which cannot be hidden, for reasons nobody in the stories explains. A figure whose one unhidable property is the thing that gives him away. Two honesty notes kept on the entry: in the magazine stories the Shadow did not become literally invisible at all, and the famous opening line is a radio adaptation's, spoken by Readick, not the print character's. And the honest placement is `made`, not `mirrored`. The Shadow is not supplied by the person who loves him; he is assembled by a publisher, an advertising agency, a writer-director and a scriptwriter, which is the same structure as `howdy-doody` eight years later - a voice first, and a figure only once somebody needs one.

src.citation: The Shadow. Wikipedia.
src.claim: The origin, the invented name and the magazine that never existed: Street & Smith Publications hired David Chrisman, of the Ruthrauff & Ryan advertising agency, and writer-director William Sweets to adapt Detective Story Magazine's stories into a radio series; they 'thought the upcoming series should be narrated by a mysterious storyteller with a sinister voice and began searching for a suitable name'; scriptwriter Harry Engman Charlot proposed the alternatives 'The Inspector' and 'The Sleuth' and then The Shadow, which was 'the name given to the mysterious narrator of the Detective Story Hour radio program' beginning 31 July 1930, first voiced by James LaCurto and replaced after four months by Frank Readick Jr. 'Although the latter company had hoped the radio broadcasts would boost the declining sales of Detective Story Magazine, the result was quite different. Listeners found the sinister announcer much more compelling than the unrelated stories. They soon began asking newsdealers for copies of "that Shadow detective magazine", even though it did not exist.' Also: in the magazine stories the Shadow did not become literally invisible, and the radio opening line - 'Who knows what evil lurks in the hearts of men? The Shadow knows!' - has earned a place in the American idiom. Powers in radio and film include turning himself invisible 'except for his shadow, which cannot be hidden, for unknown reasons'.

nodes.s: A form built almost entirely by women, for women, and treated as unserious for fifty years. Daily episodes, fixed slots, cliffhangers, characters written in indefinitely and never resolved.
nodes.g: The origin of the entire research tradition, and it started as a footnote about daytime television that nobody thought was important. The rhythm is the mechanism: a fixed slot and an unresolved story, repeated daily, is a relationship with a schedule. It is also the reason the phrase 'soap opera' is now an insult rather than a description.

src.citation: Schlesinger, P. (1932, 1933), WGN

nodes.s: A named, described character with an air of reality, kept going by being referred to. Two-thirds of children have one, most of them invisible, and a quarter of those are unknown to their parents.
nodes.g: The largest single hole in this corpus until it was counted, and the purest instance of the phenomenon the site is about: a specific person who cannot answer, held in place by nothing but consistent attention. The prevalence is the finding - in the largest systematic study 829 children, 46.2 per cent, reported imaginary companions, and a separate study put it at 65 per cent by age seven - and the composition is the argument. Among preschool children 52 per cent of companions were props, special toys; among school-age children 67 per cent were entirely invisible. 57 per cent were human, 41 per cent animals. One could transform into any animal the child wanted. And 27 per cent of the children described a friend their parents did not know about. The honesty condition is the reverse of every other entry here: the child knows they invented it, which makes this the one relationship on the site that cannot be mistaken for a misreading of somebody real. What is also documented is that they are not always kind - a number were uncontrollable and some were a nuisance - and how they end, which is that they are usually replaced rather than lost, or simply forgotten, or superseded by real friendships serving the same need. Impersonation is near-universal alongside it: 95 per cent of school-age children pretended to be a character. This is the substrate the whole site is standing on, and it was missing.

src.citation: Carlson, L. A., & Taylor, A. M. Imaginary Friends: Most kids have one (or more). University of Washington News, 9 December 2004, reporting the University of Oregon study.
src.claim: 65 per cent of children report having had an imaginary companion by age seven. Of the companions preschool children played with, 52 per cent were based on props such as special toys; of those created by school-age children, 67 per cent were invisible. 57 per cent were humans and 41 per cent animals, one being a human able to transform into any animal the child wanted. Guises included invisible boys and girls, a squirrel, a panther, a dog and a seven-inch-tall elephant. 27 per cent of the children described an imaginary friend their parents did not know about. 'Not all imaginary companions are friendly. A number were quite uncontrollable and some were a nuisance.' Impersonation was almost universal: 95 per cent of school-age children. Carlson on how they end: they 'simply go away, or children don't remember', or are replaced by new companions or by real friendships meeting the same needs.

src.citation: Pearson, D., et al. (2001). Prevalence of imaginary companions in a normal child population. Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry.
src.claim: The largest systematic study: 829 children, 46.2 per cent, reported experiences of imaginary companions. Quoted in later work as establishing that approximately 39 per cent of children aged five to seven reported an invisible imaginary companion and approximately 22 per cent of those aged eight to twelve did.

src.citation: Imaginary companions created by children who have lived in foster care. (PMC5663238)
src.claim: The prevalence range with personified objects included, and the negative result worth recording: 46 to 65 per cent of preschool and early school-age children. In this sample 26 of 60 children (43.3 per cent) reported imaginary companions, 15 invisible friends and 11 personified objects, and - the part this entry should not omit - prevalence did not differ between children with and without a history of maltreatment, consistent with retrospective data. The behaviour is common, not a marker of damage. Svendsen's 1934 definition is quoted in the related literature as the standard: an invisible character 'having an air of reality for the child, but no apparent objective basis'.

src.citation: Davis, P. E., Meins, E., & Fernyhough, C. (2013). Children with imaginary companions focus on mental characteristics when describing their real-life friends.
src.claim: The spillover, which is the part with consequences: in a sample of 159 five-year-olds, 68 (43 per cent) reported an imaginary companion, and children with one were markedly more likely to describe their real best friend in mental terms - 29.6 per cent of descriptions against 12.6 per cent for children without. The invented relationship is training the real one.

nodes.s: A character who cannot die, printed in a newspaper, read by a generation of children on the same day.
nodes.g: The first parasocial figure with an explicit immortality guarantee, which is the trade being made: I will never get over this, and I will never have to find out. Nobody has ever been made this offer in a relationship.

nodes.t: The protagonist is a parasocial object
nodes.s: The first-person film, the subjective shot, the character who exists to be looked through rather than at.
nodes.g: A technical innovation that produced a psychological one. Putting the camera inside somebody's eyes makes the audience's position structurally identical to the character's, which is the whole friendship with a film in one device.

nodes.s: Teenagers organised in public, in letterpress newsletters, to buy records and argue about a singer. A press of ten thousand.
nodes.g: The first parasocial mass movement with its own publishing, its own jargon and its own antagonism toward the parents of the people in it. Everything since is a re-skin.

src.claim: The teenage 'bobby-soxer', a term from the 1940s, and the scream that made one - the press turned a sound at a Sinatra performance into a generational diagnosis of mass hysteria. The first recorded audience parasocial event
src.citation: Bobby-soxer (Wikipedia).

nodes.s: The long-standing explanation that parasocial feeling is a projection - people attach to a figure because the figure is available to be shaped by whoever is looking.
nodes.g: Still the most intuitive theory and the least satisfying one, because it makes the relationship entirely internal to the viewer. The research moved away from it, not because projection is wrong, but because it cannot explain why a specific figure reaches a specific person and nobody else does.

nodes.s: The song where the singer pleads to be given the exact shape a man wants: a French phrase, a café in the dark. A whole musical built around wanting to be a specific imaginary person for somebody.
nodes.g: The template for a large fraction of the twentieth century. Cole Porter did not invent the impulse, he published it, and the song is still the most precise description of the thing that every subsequent song about obsessive attachment is a worse version of.
