src.citation: Porter, C. (1943). 'Gigi'.

nodes.s: Made to answer a four-year-old's fear of the dark, by a man who made a cardboard cutout and hung it in a tree. Two men then claimed to have invented him.
nodes.g: The `haunted` shelf opened by the reason the shelf exists. Casper is a ghost whose entire design brief was to be verifiable-in-principle and safe in fact: according to Joe Oriolo, he was made on a Halloween night to assuage his four-year-old daughter Joan's fear of the dark, as a cardboard cutout of a friendly ghost hung in the backyard tree to show her that not all ghosts are bad. A ghost built as an intervention against a specific fear, for one named child, is the most parasocial brief a supernatural figure has ever had - and the child's side of it is checkable, which is the only part of the story that is. Then the commercial part. Casper ran from 1945, and the character ended up in Harvey Comics, in television and in feature films, which means the figure that answered one girl's fear of the dark became a property that could be licensed. The site keeps two honesty notes. The first is that **the origin is genuinely disputed**: Oriolo claims the cardboard cutout, his daughter has corroborated it, and Seymour Reit maintains Casper was born with a short story he conceived and wrote entirely himself and handed to Oriolo to illustrate - 'Joe created the actual cartoon of the character - but the concept, series, idea and plotline were mine, prior to Joe's involvement.' A corpus that files contested authorship under a single name would be lying, so both are recorded. The second is that `haunted` is defined on belief in presence, not on the supernatural: Casper is not filed as a ghost story but as a figure a child was prepared to believe in, which is a different and more useful thing. The most parasocial detail is the one nobody chose: the Apollo 16 command and service module was given the call sign Casper, because its pilot Ken Mattingly thought 'there are enough serious things in this flight, so I picked a non-serious name.' A friendly dead child's ghost ended up naming a spacecraft in orbit.

src.citation: Casper the Friendly Ghost. Wikipedia.
src.claim: First appearance as 'The Friendly Ghost', 16 November 1945; creators credited as Seymour Reit, Joe Oriolo and Vincent E. Valentine II. On the disputed origin: 'The origins of Casper are disputed, with both Seymour Reit and Joe Oriolo claiming to be the character's creator. According to Oriolo, Casper was created on a Halloween night to assuage his four-year-old daughter Joan's fear of the dark. He made a cardboard cutout of a friendly ghost and hung it in the backyard tree to show her that not all ghosts are bad.' 'Though Joan has corroborated this story, Seymour Reit maintains that Casper was born with a short story which he conceived and wrote entirely by himself and gave to Oriolo to illustrate. Reit concluded, "Joe created the actual cartoon of the character - but the concept, series, idea and plotline were mine, prior to Joe's involvement."' And the call sign: 'The Apollo 16 Command and Service Module was given the call sign "Casper", since its pilot Ken Mattingly thought, "there are enough serious things in this flight, so I picked a non-serious name."'

src.citation: Orlando, J. D. 'Cartoonist Joseph D. Oriolo, Creator of Casper the Ghost.' Chicago Tribune, 27 December 1985.

nodes.t: Say, kids, what time is it?
nodes.s: The first television character to be answered by name. Children three to eight shouted its name back at the screen every afternoon for thirteen years, and the puppet it was played by was recorded before the broadcast.
nodes.g: The template for every children's presenter since, and the purest mechanism on this site: a figure that talks to you, built by somebody else, delivered from tape. Buffalo Bob Smith first performed Howdy Doody as a radio voice; Frank Paris built a puppet to match it; when Paris left in 1948 over merchandising rights he took the original puppet with him and the replacement debuted that June. For thirteen years and some 2,500 episodes the show opened on the same transaction - 'Say, kids, what time is it?' answered, in unison, 'It's Howdy Doody time!' - which is a named individual greeted daily by name by a room of children who could not have told you who was operating him, since the voice was usually recorded before the show. Two details do more work than the format. Clarabell the Clown never spoke for twelve years, communicating with a horn and a seltzer bottle, and said his first and only line in the final episode: 'Good-bye, kids.' A silent character choosing to speak, once, at the end. And the puppet left the screen: Howdy Doody marionettes with sliding eyes and moving mouths were sold as toys throughout the 1950s, so the relationship moved from a thing you cannot touch to an object in your hands. That is the whole thesis of this site in one commercial decision, and it was made before most of the people reading it were born.

src.citation: Howdy Doody. Wikipedia.
src.claim: Broadcast on NBC from 27 December 1947 to 24 September 1960. Howdy Doody was originally only a voice performed by Buffalo Bob Smith on radio; when Smith appeared on NBC's Puppet Playhouse on 27 December 1947 the reception was great enough to demand a visual character, and puppeteer Frank Paris was asked to create the puppet.

src.citation: Howdy Doody Show. EBSCO Research Starters, History.
src.claim: The daily transaction, the audience, and the ending: at the beginning of every show Buffalo Bob asked his child audience in the Peanut Gallery bleachers 'Say, kids, what time is it?' and the children shouted 'It's Howdy Doody time!' Roughly 2,500 episodes aired 1947-1960. Clarabell the Clown communicated by honking a horn and squirting a seltzer bottle, and in the final episode the silent clown spoke for the first time: 'Good-bye, kids.'

src.citation: Howdy Doody marionette. National Museum of American History, Smithsonian Institution (NMAH 670111).
src.claim: That the figure was worked by somebody the audience never saw, and from tape: throughout the NBC run 'Bob Smith voiced the puppet, usually through recordings made before the show, while Margo and Rufus Rose were primarily responsible for building, maintaining, and performing the marionettes'. Also the puppet's own instability: in 1948 a dispute over merchandising rights led Frank Paris to leave the show and take the original puppet with him, and Velma Dawson's replacement debuted on 8 June 1948 after a break for 'plastic surgery'. Publisher returns 403 to an unauthenticated request.

nodes.g: The clearest case of the bond forming after the person withdrew from it, and of the work becoming the only place the relationship could continue.

nodes.g: The first institutional form, and the origin of nearly everything downstream including the paid tiers. The important part is that fans built a lot of it themselves, which is the strongest evidence that the impulse is real and the structure is optional.

nodes.t: Nobody in that room argues with him
nodes.s: A man nobody else can see kept drinking with him for years, and it worked because nobody in his life would say the sentence that ended it. It stops when two doctors who cannot see the rabbit go looking for him in it.
nodes.g: The purest `haunted` case in film, and the clearest demonstration of the thing the whole film is actually about, which is not the rabbit. Elwood P. Dowd has an invisible companion six foot three and a half inches tall, and takes him drinking and introduces him to almost everyone he meets. The mechanism that keeps this intact is **not** the animal. It is the **complicity of the people around him**, and the film is unusually honest about how cheap that complicity is. His sister Veta "in exasperation, admits to the attending psychiatrist, Dr. Sanderson, that she sees Harvey once in a while herself" - which is not the same as seeing him, and is not meant to be, and is enough for her to be committed in Elwood's place while he walks out free. Dr. Chumley, the head of the sanatorium, discovers the mistake, convinced that Elwood is insane, searches the town for him, finds him at his favourite bar - and then, four hours later, "Chumley had wandered off with Harvey after several rounds of drinks." The professional sent to certify the delusion goes off with the delusion. Every bond in this corpus needs somebody to maintain it, and this one is maintained by the fact that **nobody will say the sentence.** Elwood's belief costs nothing as long as everyone around him declines to price it. Three more things make it the right entry and not merely a nice one. The rabbit is not a rabbit: Elwood describes Harvey as a **puca**, a creature of Celtic mythology, and the play spells it *pookah* (p-o-o-k-a) with the character Wilson reading the definition aloud from a dictionary on page 33 of Chase's playbook - so even the ontology is a thing somebody made up and passed on. Wikipedia's own summary of the source hedges exactly as an encyclopedia should: Elwood "claims to have an unseen (and presumably imaginary) friend", and a neutral reference hedging is worth more than a confident one. And the performance is layered further than most people notice: a real man playing a man who is trusted, who converses with a thing nobody else in the room can see, while the audience half-believes him because James Stewart's face is doing work no script controls. Two corrections to the record while we are here, because they were nearly got wrong: the 1950 film was directed by **Henry Koster**, not Cukor, and Mary Chase's play is **1944**, premiered 1 November 1944 at the 48th Street Theatre, with the Pulitzer Prize for Drama awarded 1945 - not 1946, which several sources imply.

src.citation: Harvey (1950 film). Wikipedia.
src.claim: Director, cast and the whole premise: 'Harvey is a 1950 American fantasy comedy-drama film directed by Henry Koster, based on the 1944 play by Mary Chase. It stars James Stewart, Josephine Hull, Charles Drake, Cecil Kellaway, Jesse White, Victoria Horne, Wallace Ford, and Peggy Dow.' Elwood P. Dowd 'is an amiable but eccentric man whose best friend is an invisible, 6 ft 3 1/2 in-tall (1.92 m) white rabbit named Harvey. As described by Elwood, Harvey is a puca, a benign but mischievous creature from Celtic mythology.' Elwood 'spends most of his time taking Harvey around town, drinking at various bars and introducing Harvey to almost everyone he meets, much to the puzzlement of strangers although Elwood's friends have accepted Harvey's (supposed) existence.' Veta 'finally tries to have him committed to a local sanatorium. In exasperation, she admits to the attending psychiatrist, Dr. Sanderson, that she sees Harvey once in a while herself. Mistaking Veta for the real mental case, Sanderson has Elwood released and Veta locked up.' Chumley 'eventually tracks Elwood to his favorite bar, Charlie's, and confronts him. Four hours later, Wilson returns to the sanatorium and learns from Sanderson and nurse Kelly that Chumley and Elwood had not returned... they all go to Charlie's and find Elwood alone; he explains that Chumley wandered off with Harvey after several rounds of drinks.'

src.citation: Harvey (play). Wikipedia.
src.claim: The play's dates and its hedge: 'Harvey is a 1944 play by the American playwright Mary Chase, who received the Pulitzer Prize for Drama for the work in 1945', Broadway premiere 1 November 1944 at the 48th Street Theatre, settings 'The library of the Old Dowd Mansion' and 'The Reception Room at Chumley's Rest'. And the spelling, which is the detail that makes the ontology deliberate: Elwood 'claims to have an unseen (and presumably imaginary) friend Harvey - whom Elwood describes as a six foot, three-and-one-half inch pookah (Chase uses the spelling p-o-o-k-a as noted especially by the character Wilson who is reading the definition from a dictionary on page 33 of Chase's playbook)'.

nodes.s: A person who recognises you, remembers what you wanted, and has the right thing behind the counter when you come back.
nodes.g: The origin of the site mascot and the most parasocial job in retail, which nobody has ever written a paper about. It is also the most useful control condition: the same attention, delivered by a person who gets paid to give it.

nodes.s: One person on your own television, in your own town, for twenty years, who is leaving and everybody is upset.
nodes.g: Rubin's longitudinal work is on exactly this bond. When a local anchor retires the grief is measurable and there is no word for it, because a parasocial relationship with a local figure is assumed to be about the news rather than about the person.

nodes.s: Someone whose kitchen light you can see, whose bin day you know, and whose life you have been tracking for years without ever having asked.
nodes.g: A parasocial bond with somebody who is physically present and therefore, apparently, cannot be the subject of one. The reasoning is that proximity disqualifies attachment, which is exactly backwards and is why Section 07 was empty for so long.

src.claim: The canonical account of why proximity without contact produces a relationship at all: weak ties carry information and feelings that strong ties cannot, and the value of an acquaintance is precisely that it is un-demanded
src.citation: Granovetter, M. S. (1973). The Strength of Weak Ties. American Journal of Sociology, 78(6), 1360-1380.

src.citation: Sennett, R. The Conscience of the Eye: The Architecture and Morality of Public Space.

nodes.s: A sales clerk who remembered. Not a recommendation engine, not a loyalty points balance - a person who noticed what you had looked at and had the right thing ready when you came back.
nodes.g: The historical control condition. Every 'personalised' retail system since is an attempt to reproduce what one person could do for a few hundred regulars, and none of them have done it as well, because the thing that made it work was not the data. It was that it was somebody's job to pay attention.

nodes.s: A national simultaneous viewing event, and an industry that learned within two years that the appeal was not the music.

nodes.s: The name itself. Coined to describe the way viewers responded to a television character they followed consistently - a bond with somebody who did not know they existed. Parasocial: one-sided, parallel to the para- in paranormal.
nodes.g: The coinage is defensive and that is the story. It was invented in the McCarthy era to describe a television habit that was considered slightly shameful - viewers writing in about soap characters as though they could be defamed. The word bakes in an apology for the feeling. The feeling did not need one.

nodes.g: The first documented case of a parasocial attachment being designed as a manufacturing process. The product is the bond, and it has a launch date.

He had been a screen presence since birth playing himself in his parents' weekly series, which is the whole supply chain: the attachment preceded the product and was then monetised through it.

nodes.s: A recurring family, played by the same cast, five nights a week, for years, in a house you could draw from memory.
nodes.g: Attachment to a fictional household, watched nightly, in the pre-internet equivalent of a comfort rewatch. Research on sitcom parasocial attachment found the same pattern as soaps: it is the accumulation, not the plot.

src.claim: N=840: appreciation and enjoyment are separate responses. Appreciation is being moved; enjoyment is pleasure. Tragic outcomes still produce appreciation even where enjoyment is absent - the family you miss was never the fun one
src.citation: Krakowiak, K. M. (2024). How It Ends: Exploring How Narrative Closure and Character Outcomes in Series Finales Relate to Viewer Responses and Coping Behaviors.

src.claim: And the mechanism that makes loss social: appreciation INCREASED coping behaviours - seeking more information, reading analyses, discussing with other viewers - while enjoyment decreased them. Feeling moved makes you go and talk to someone
src.citation: Krakowiak, K. M. (2024). How It Ends.

nodes.s: Support for a politician structured as a personal bond rather than a policy preference, in a way that transfers poorly across candidates.
nodes.g: The oldest public parasocial bond is the sovereign, and it is the one the field has consistently declined to study. A stadium and a parliament are the same room with different seating plans.

src.claim: the entry as a whole
src.citation: Spectator Australia, 2026

nodes.s: She received correspondence by the sackful and answered it by name, individually, for years. The closest thing the twentieth century produced to a genuinely reciprocal parasocial relationship.
nodes.g: The proof that reciprocity is possible and therefore a choice, not a law of nature. Every subsequent complaint that the parasocial relationship has no reply is answering a question she had already settled.

src.claim: the entry as a whole
src.citation: Warwick, D. (1994). Memories of a lifetime.

nodes.s: A global mass hysteria, documented live, with screaming, fainting, and an industry that began pricing it within months.
nodes.g: The first time the world watched itself develop a parasocial disorder in real time, and the first time anybody seriously proposed monetising it. The licensing of merchandising set the template for everything since.

src.claim: THE FIRST FAN BEHAVIOUR MEASURED RATHER THAN DIAGNOSED. 346 subjects aged 15-20, tested shortly after the Beatles' Wellington visit, split into 50 keenest, 122 moderate, 50 'resisters'. The authors found NO evidence on the MMPI Hysteria Scale and no supporting clinical evidence of neuroticism, and teachers reported none needed referral
src.citation: Taylor, A. J. W. (1966). Beatlemania - A Study in Adolescent Enthusiasm. British Journal of Social and Clinical Psychology, 5(2), 81-88.

src.claim: Their conclusion, quoted in the abstract: Beatlemania is 'the passing reaction of predominantly young adolescent females to group pressures of such a kind that meet their special emotional needs.' Developmentally real, not clinically
src.citation: Taylor, A. J. W. (1966). Beatlemania - A Study in Adolescent Enthusiasm.

src.claim: What the fans said the apparatus was. First-generation fan Candy Leonard, now a scholar of it: 'the mags were a way to extend/enhance the experience... We saw the Beatles as extended family and that was the way to keep up with them. The records, the transistor radio, the merch, the conversation, and the magazines created what I call a wraparound experience'
src.citation: Bumsted, A. 1960s Teen Fan Magazines and The Beatles, interviews with first-generation fan Candy Leonard.

src.claim: The turn, dated by a fan to a record: Leonard places the change at Rubber Soul (December 1965), the moment 'the Beatles came to occupy a role in fans' lives and a place in their psyches that was different from any previous fan-performer relationship'
src.citation: Candy Leonard, Beatleness: George Beatles and the Beatles' Legacy (2014).

src.claim: The hostile framing, for the ledger: Paul Johnson wrote in the New Statesman in February 1964 that the mania was a modern incarnation of female hysteria and that the fans at their concerts were 'the least fortunate of their generation, the dull, the idle, the failures'. It became the most complained-about piece in that magazine's history
src.citation: Beatlemania (Wikipedia), citing Paul Johnson, New Statesman, February 1964.

src.claim: The sympathetic reading, from the period: Ehrenreich, Hess and Jacobs argued Beatlemania was the first mass outburst of the sixties to feature women, girls who would not reach full adulthood until the seventies, and therefore 'the emergence of a genuinely political movement for women's liberation'
src.citation: Ehrenreich, B., Hess, E., & Jacobs, G. (1986). Re-making Love: The Feminization of Sex.

src.claim: And the reading that got there first: a 1997 study argued Beatlemania represented proto-feminist girl power, anticipating by thirty years what the archive would show
src.citation: Beatlemania: A sexually defiant consumer subculture? (1997).

src.claim: The band press officer's summary, offered as flattery and accurate anyway: Derek Taylor described the relationship between the Beatles and their fans as 'the twentieth century's greatest romance'
src.citation: Beatlemania (Wikipedia), citing Derek Taylor.

nodes.s: A short pattern-matching script that reflects the user's words back with questions attached. Most people told it they understood, within minutes.
nodes.g: The founding demonstration that an attentive-seeming system is enough, and that the belief is generated by the response rather than by the intelligence behind it. Every companion app since is a bigger ELIZA, and the field has still not fully absorbed what that first one proved.

src.claim: the entry as a whole
src.citation: Weizenbaum, 1966

nodes.s: ELIZA, PARRY and Colby - three programs that convinced people they were listening.
nodes.g: All three were written to be good enough to be believed, and the belief was studied as a phenomenon rather than treated as a bug.

src.claim: Weizenbaum (ELIZA), Colby (PARRY), and Colby's follow-up work.
src.citation: Standard history of early natural-language programs, 1966-1975.

nodes.s: Research on why some political candidates reliably produce personal attachment and others do not, despite comparable policy positions.
nodes.g: If charisma is a real and learnable thing, then attachment to public figures is manipulable by design, and the manipulation is not a side effect of the work.

src.claim: The classical account of charisma as a political asset, and of its built-in instability: Weber's charismatic authority rests on devotion to the exceptional person rather than on rules or office, which is precisely why it cannot be institutionalised without being transformed
src.citation: Weber, M. Economy and Society ( posthumous, 1922), on charismatic authority and its routinisation.

src.claim: Weber's warning is the useful part for this site: charisma is understood to be unstable and to require routinisation into something impersonal, which is the same bargain described here from the other end
src.citation: Weber, M. Economy and Society.

nodes.s: The fictional thing rents space in someone's head and starts paying rent in meaning. You rehearse the encounters, you decorate them, you introduce them to friends like a roommate.
nodes.g: Fiction is the safest place on earth to find out what you actually feel, because nothing in there can disappoint you on purpose. The only line worth drawing is where the room starts making house rules - when the lore thread replaces the friend, or the edit replaces sleep. That line is always felt long before it can be explained.

src.claim: A fictional character who moves into your home and stays: Mr. Belvedere, an English butler employed as a live-in housekeeper by an American family, 1985-1990, 117 episodes. He is nursemaid, cook, cleaner, confidant and conscience, and he never leaves until the finale
src.citation: Mr. Belvedere (Wikipedia).

src.claim: AND THE DEVICE THAT MAKES IT PARASOCIAL RATHER THAN SITCOM: every episode ends with Belvedere writing in his journal, giving the moral and putting the week's events in perspective. The character keeps a diary about the family - and about the audience watching him keep it
src.citation: Mr. Belvedere - Plot (IMDb).

src.claim: The setting was fabricated wholesale: the producers had never visited Pittsburgh, worked from a promotional calendar, and shot no scenes there. The household is a set of rooms in a place that does not exist
src.citation: Mr. Belvedere (Wikipedia), reporting Dungan and Stein.

src.claim: And the exit, which is the point: in the two-part finale he marries and moves to Africa, leaving the family. The character that moved in eventually has to leave, and the audience is not consulted
src.citation: Mr. Belvedere - Premise (Liquisearch).

src.claim: THE MECHANISM, STATED PLAINLY BY SOMEONE MEASURING IT: stories and story characters provide interpersonal intimacy WITHOUT THE THREAT OF REJECTION. That is the whole reason a fictional figure can be safer than a person
src.citation: Rain, M., & Mar, R. A. (2021). Adult attachment and engagement with fictional characters.

src.claim: And it is conditional, which is the uncomfortable part: attachment anxiety and avoidance DIFFERENTIALLY predict character identification and parasocial interaction, and a high-powered pre-registered follow-up found attachment orientation predicts which characters people are drawn to. Some characters are wanted because they are unavailable
src.citation: Rain & Mar (2021).

src.claim: Sometimes you are not watching the character, you ARE it - and the literature distinguishes the two. A player-avatar relationship can be MONADIC, where the player identifies with the avatar to the point of being the same being, or DYADIC, where a separation makes it closer to a parasocial relationship. Same apparatus, opposite structure
src.citation: Ferchaud, A. (2024). Identification and Parasocial Relationships With Video Game Characters. Oxford Research Encyclopedia of Communication.

src.claim: What it takes linguistically, from interviews with MMO players: SELF-DIFFERENTIATION and ANTHROPOMORPHIZATION together suspend disbelief enough for the figure to be taken as a fully social agent. You have to make it different from you and also human, at the same time
src.citation: Avatars are (sometimes) people too: Linguistic indicators of parasocial and social ties in player-avatar relationships. New Media & Society.

src.claim: The bond once mistaken for pathology is ordinary attachment style: research on intimate television viewing shows people forming relationships parasocially and insecurely, and treats it as a predictable outcome of disposition rather than a malfunction
src.citation: Cole, T., & Leets, L. (1999). Attachment Styles and Intimate Television Viewing: Insecurely Forming Relationships in a Parasocial Way. Journal of Social and Personal Relationships, 16(4), 495-511.

src.claim: And the predictable ending, named in the literature: parasocial break-up from favourite television characters is studied as its own phenomenon, driven by attachment style and relationship intensity rather than by anything the character did
src.citation: Cohen, J. (2004). Parasocial Break-Up from Favorite Television Characters: The Role of Attachment Styles and Relationship Intensity. Journal of Social and Personal Relationships, 21(2), 187-202.

src.claim: THE ABSENT REPLY, WHICH IS THE WHOLE ARGUMENT IN 1774. Werther writes to his friend Wilhelm but the reader never sees Wilhelm's replies - the letters are missing. The reader therefore becomes Wilhelm's stand-in and must supply the response themselves. An 18th-century readership expecting an explicit moral from the narrator is instead left to answer for a character who cannot answer
src.citation: Goethe's Werther and its effects. The Lancet Psychiatry (2014).

src.claim: But the epidemic is NOT established, and the site's honesty requires saying so: a systematic search of German, Austrian and Swiss newspaper databases since 1774 found eight previously undocumented suicides the press connected to the novel, while the papers themselves reported the 'Werther-epidemic' and its moral implications far more than individual imitative suicides. Whether it substantiates an epidemic remains up to interpretation
src.citation: Anecdotal Evidence in Historical News Reports (2023), reviewing suicides the press connected to Goethe's Werther since 1774.

src.claim: There is a counter-effect and it has a name too: the Papageno effect, after Mozart's character in The Magic Flute, in which portrayals of a character contemplating suicide who is prevented at the last moment reduce imitation. Media reporting guidelines exist for both. The mechanism runs in both directions and the site should not pretend otherwise
src.citation: Goethe's Werther and its effects. The Lancet Psychiatry (2014), discussing the Werther and Papageno effects.

src.claim: Byron called Goethe 'the first literary character in Europe' fifty years later, and Napoleon read the novel seven times before discussing it with its author in 1808
src.citation: Goethe's Werther and its effects. The Lancet Psychiatry (2014), citing Bayard Quincy Morgan.

src.claim: The register that this whole project is about, stated by the author: when he finished it Goethe likened his mood to being 'after a general confession, joyous and free and entitled to a new life'. For Goethe the Werther effect was cathartic. Not so for its readers
src.citation: Goethe's Werther and its effects. The Lancet Psychiatry (2014), citing David Constantine's introduction to his translation.

nodes.t: Grieving a person you never met
nodes.s: Collective mourning of a public figure, and the persistent argument about whether it counts. Measured in studies of soap opera finales finding grief markers the same shape as the end of a relationship.
nodes.g: The largest and most defensible category on this site. Losing somebody is what happens when the people you love die, and a very large number of people grieve in public and are told it is a symptom. The only unusual thing about parasocial grief is that the person could not have known you were there, and that deserves care rather than condescension.

src.claim: Parasocial grief is real, measurable, and specifically disenfranchised: a death the world does not recognise as a loss
src.citation: DeGroot, J. M., & Leith, A. P. (2018). R.I.P. Kutner: Parasocial Grief Following the Death of a Television Character. Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly, 77(3), 199-216.

src.claim: Grief at the end of a long series, measured at scale (n=1289) after the Neighbours finale
src.citation: Gerace, A. (2024). When TV neighbours become good friends: Understanding Neighbours fans' feelings of grief and loss at the end of the series. PLOS ONE.

src.claim: Character death and series cancellation produce similar distress; voluntary withdrawal produces much less
src.citation: Cuddy, L., & Ellithorpe, M. E. (2025). 'I was Absolutely Devastated at This Death': Refining the Conceptualization and Processes of Parasocial Breakup Distress.

src.claim: Mourning is conducted on Facebook RIP pages for people the mourner never met
src.citation: Klastrup, L. (2015). 'I didn't know her, but...': Parasocial mourning of mediated deaths on Facebook RIP pages. New Review of Hypermedia and Multimedia.

src.claim: The framework's founding measurement of parasocial breakup
src.citation: Eyal, K., & Cohen, J. (2006). When Good Friends Say Goodbye: A Parasocial Breakup Study. Journal of Broadcasting & Electronic Media, 50(3), 502-523.

src.claim: Grief outcomes after a real celebrity death, and the role of parasocial relations in stigma and help-seeking
src.citation: Hoffner, C. A., & Cohen, E. L. (2017). Mental Health-Related Outcomes of Robin Williams' Death. Health Communication, 33(12), 1573-1582.

src.claim: THE CONTESTED CLAIM: relational closeness, not parasociality, predicts grief intensity at celebrity death - i.e. the grief is not the parasocial bond
src.citation: Baker, A. C., & Cohen, E. L. (2023). Relational closeness - not parasociality - determines the intensity of grief responses to celebrity death. Death Studies, 48(8), 873-878.

nodes.s: A conversational system about a small blocks world, capable of genuinely tracking a user's intentions. Famous for one demonstration and a broken follow-up.
nodes.g: The proof that machine understanding of intent was considered a solved research problem in 1970 and has been failing privately ever since. The person who made SHRDLU then said the problem was far harder than it looked, and was believed by nobody.

src.claim: the entry as a whole
src.citation: Winograd, 1970

nodes.s: Fans gather, in costume, in a hotel ballroom, to be in the same room with people who feel the same way about a show.
nodes.g: The first mass physical assembly of parasocial people, and the proof that the bond had become a social fact requiring infrastructure. Everything after is logistics.

src.claim: The first Star Trek convention, 3-5 March 1972 at the Hotel Commodore in New York, organised largely by James Doohan and his wife, drew a crowd far larger than the organisers had expected and is the direct ancestor of the modern comics convention
src.citation: Star Trek Convention (Wikipedia).

nodes.t: Elvis, in a hologram, from Hawaii
nodes.s: Elvis Presley was filmed in a two-dimensional process that placed an apparently three-dimensional Elvis on stage, in a scene where real people were supposed to react to him. Aloha from Hawaii via Satellite reached an estimated half the planet.
nodes.g: The first parasocial technology, and it makes the argument nobody wanted to make. It was simultaneously beloved, a triumph, and a demonstration that you can attach to a projection on purpose. Everything since - deepfakes, holograms, an AI voice reading a dead actor's lines - is a lateral move from here.

src.claim: the entry as a whole
src.citation: Aloha from Hawaii via Satellite, 1973

nodes.s: Fan conventions as a permanent global circuit, with panels, dealers rooms, cosplay and a trade layer.
nodes.g: The first parasocial economy. Panels are a person answering questions from an audience that has paid to be in the room, and the dealers room is the first marketplace that exists because of the bond rather than beside it.

src.claim: Comic fandom built its own institution: the Golden State Comic-Con held its first convention in 1970 in a hotel ballroom in San Diego, organised by a group of fans, with Ray Bradbury as the first programme guest. The convention is the fandom's own building
src.citation: San Diego Comic-Con (Wikipedia).

nodes.t: The finding that the satisfaction is not in the show
nodes.s: Across several decades of television studies the same pair of results kept surfacing: these bonds are extremely common among regular viewers, and the strength of the bond predicts enjoyment better than the quality of the programme does.
nodes.g: It says the satisfaction is not in the writing, it is in the accumulation. A show that is not very good, watched consistently, produces a stronger feeling than a good show watched occasionally. This is why commitment to a mediocre series is not a failure of taste, and it is the most consistently replicated and least widely known finding in the entire field.

src.claim: the entry as a whole
src.citation: No single source identified yet; this entry needs its individual studies added.

nodes.s: A television film made for a fictional holiday, aired once, about characters the audience believed they owned.
nodes.g: The strangest parasocial document in the file. An entire fictional religion, complete with costume, was made for an audience that had formed a genuine attachment, and that audience watched it and understood it as a gift.

src.claim: Life Day, the Star Wars holiday special, was broadcast on CBS on 17 November 1978 - a holiday invented for a film series, given a network slot, and later quietly dropped. The franchise built a calendar
src.citation: Life Day (Wikipedia).

nodes.s: The unsettling quality of a humanlike thing that is not human, and the narrow band where it is most compelling.
nodes.g: Predicts the companion era accurately. Too obviously a machine and it is a tool; too obviously a person and it is a person. The uncanny valley is also the commercial sweet spot, which is a genuinely uncomfortable sentence to write.

src.claim: the entry as a whole
src.citation: Mori, 1979

nodes.s: Academic work measuring grief responses to soap opera finales and finding the same markers as bereavement.
nodes.g: The first hard evidence that a fictional ending produces a real grief response, and the research that was ignored for forty years by a field that had assumed otherwise.

src.claim: the entry as a whole
src.citation: ABC News, 2023

nodes.s: Stories resolve on a fixed date, the wait is publicised in advance, and the audience is given a date to be in the same place at the same time.
nodes.g: The modern ritual version of the serial. A year-long shared countdown, with the entire audience aimed at one moment, is the parasocial equivalent of a religious festival and functions identically.

src.claim: A randomized trial: 44 children assigned to serial (cliffhanger) or episodic delivery of the same story. Serial held engagement across visits; episodic's 'temporary relief' REDUCED long-term play. Unresolved tension beat temporary resolution
src.citation: To Pause With a Cliffhanger or a Temporary Closure: Serial vs. episodic narratives and sustained engagement.

src.claim: A cliffhanger is defined in the literature as unresolved tension created specifically to motivate audiences to return to the next episode - the seasonal form of the conduit's promise
src.citation: To Pause With a Cliffhanger or a Temporary Closure (citing Baranowski et al. 2008; Wirz et al. 2022).

src.claim: Even failing shows gain viewers for the finale; people who had already stopped watching tune in to find out how it ends. Series finales and Super Bowls are the most-watched broadcasts in US TV history
src.citation: McCormick, C. TV finales and the meaning of endings (doctoral dissertation).

nodes.s: Reward miles accrue against travel with an airline, and status is conferred by volume.
nodes.g: Status tiers are the parasocial structure with the least romance in it and the most engineering. Tier is a relationship with a company, modelled on rank, and the language of elite is the same language as devotion.

src.citation: AAdvantage. Wikipedia, citing 'A History of US Airline Deregulation Part 4: 1979-2010: The Effects of Deregulation - Lower Fares, More Travel, Frequent Flier Programs'.
src.claim: Corrects the entry's date. American launched AAdvantage on 1 May 1981, and it was the *second* such programme in the world, the first being at Texas International Airlines in 1979 - so the entry was two years late. Also the founding detail the entry was standing on top of without describing: membership began by invitation only, and 'membership was seeded by searching American's SABRE computer reservations system for recurring phone numbers', with the 130,000 most frequent flyers plus 60,000 Admirals Club members pre-enrolled and sent letters with their new account numbers, the reward being a first-class ticket to any destination American flew. United launched Mileage Plus within weeks, described as the first *modern* frequent flyer programme; AAdvantage was the first to partner with an international carrier, in 1982.

src.citation: History of United Airlines. Wikipedia (Mileage Plus, May 1981).
src.claim: The competitive clock that made the tier system urgent: in May 1981, 'a week after rival American Airlines launched AAdvantage, the first modern frequent flyer program, United launched its Mileage Plus'. Two programmes within days of each other, after which the Wikipedia AAdvantage history notes competition on features began - rules liberalised, hotel and rental partnerships, triple miles from 1988 - which is how a loyalty scheme acquires the language of rank.

nodes.s: A discount card that identifies the household, tracks what it buys, and targets offers at what it has already bought.
nodes.g: The loyalty card joins the account to the person. Everything the field calls the attention economy was operational and profitable in supermarkets a decade before anybody named it.

nodes.s: Twenty-eight million people watched a television finale and the largest audience for a broadcast in history.
nodes.g: The high-water mark of collective parasocial grief in broadcast television, watched by people who had never met a single person in it. Everything since has been smaller and more numerous.

src.claim: 'Goodbye, Farewell and Amen' aired 28 February 1983 and drew roughly 105.9 million viewers, about 38 per cent of American households - the most-watched finale in television history at the time. Directed by Alan Alda
src.citation: Goodbye, Farewell and Amen (Wikipedia); Nielsen ratings as reported contemporaneously.

src.claim: A comedy about war that closed by resolving its central question - Korea, the protagonist, the goodbye - and was watched by a third of the country
src.citation: M*A*S*H (TV series) (Wikipedia).

nodes.s: The person who knows you is also the person who profits from you, and is paid to be there, and goes home at six. The relationship has an employer.
nodes.g: The distinction nobody makes: a parasocial bond feels the same whether the other end is a person, a corporation, a platform or a state. The counter sits between the two, and that middle is where the ethics live. It is also why the video store clerk is the right mascot for a site about this.

nodes.s: A clinical name for a case where a one-sided bond is causing significant distress or impairment. Named in the eighties, and it is a real diagnosis for a small number of people.
nodes.g: The trouble is that the disorder and the ordinary bond are the same shape. The disorder requires distress - which means you cannot identify it from the strength of the feeling alone, only by asking what it is costing. That distinction is the whole point, and it is the one most coverage of the subject skips.

src.claim: the entry as a whole
src.citation: Rubin, A. M., McVoy, S. M., & Brannan, D. (1985).

nodes.s: A long-running body of work from Rubin and colleagues, repeatedly finding that people form parasocial bonds with news anchors, and that the strongest predictor of which anchor they bond with is not the anchor's performance.
nodes.g: The finding that broke the standard worry. The parasocial relationship is a substitute for interpersonal contact, not a symptom of pathology, and it does not correlate with poor mental health in the way the disorder framing implies. It is closer to a coping strategy that mostly works.

src.claim: the entry as a whole
src.citation: Rubin, A. M., McVoy, S. M., & Brannan, D. (1985). Human Communication Research, 12(2).

nodes.t: So many people want to believe he's real
nodes.s: An alien with a kitchen and a family, performed by a man who refused for four years to say how. Children cried when it ended, and the character was invited to birthday parties.
nodes.g: The case that proves the third axis needs a rule, because ALF is on two shelves at once and pretending otherwise would be the exact error the axis was built to stop. On the evidence he is `animate`: he has a mind the audience cannot edit, he wants things for himself (the cat), he is stated to be over two hundred and twenty years old, and he crash-lands because he followed a radio signal. On the evidence of his body he is `made`. Paul Fusco performed him inside a fur suit and guardianship of the mechanism so total that the Los Angeles Times described it as a magician refusing to reveal how his tricks work - 'When Alf walks, he looks like a 3-year-old in a bear costume toddling down the hallway', and in close-up 'it looks as if he could have several human hands stuck up his backside, mechanically moving his mouth, arms and body.' Full-body shots were performed by Michu Meszaros, uncredited. What makes it more than a technique note is that the withholding was deliberate and stated as method: 'Fusco insists that many people believe in Alf just as they believe in Santa Claus, and he is not about to spoil the illusion. So many people want to believe he's real. Alf is in fact very real to me. He has his own dressing room. He speaks for himself. I prefer to preserve that. When you know how it's done, it's just not as fascinating anymore.' That is this site's thesis in a performer talking about his own job: the audience's belief is the asset, and explaining the mechanism destroys it. The evidence that it worked is in the same piece: ALF 'is so fascinating and so realistic, in fact, that he gets invited to birthday parties nearly every day. And mothers have told cast members that their children cry every Monday night when Alf ends.' A character invented on paper in 1982, turned down for four years, then given a family, a pet to want and a government to hide from - and the one-sidedness is asymmetric on purpose. The Tanners are reciprocated; the cat is not; and ALF's own arc is the only one in the corpus that is about being afraid of being sent home.

src.citation: Weinstein, S. 'Alf: The Star Trek of NBC's Furry Resident Alien: How a Wisecracking Puppet Toddled Into the Hearts of Viewers.' Los Angeles Times, 23 December 1987.
src.claim: The performance and the deliberate withholding, quoted: Fusco 'guards the secret of how Alf walks and talks and moves around a desk or a television set like a magician refusing to reveal the secret of his magic tricks. When Alf walks, he looks like a 3-year-old in a bear costume toddling down the hallway. When he sits around spouting his brash opinions like a teen-age Archie Bunker, it looks as if he could have several human hands stuck up his backside, mechanically moving his mouth, arms and body.' And: 'Fusco insists that many people believe in Alf just as they believe in Santa Claus, and he is not about to spoil the illusion. "So many people want to believe he's real," Fusco says. "Alf is in fact very real to me. He has his own dressing room. He speaks for himself. I prefer to preserve that. When you know how it's done, it's just not as fascinating anymore."' Plus the evidence it worked: 'Alf is so fascinating and so realistic, in fact, that he gets invited to birthday parties nearly every day. And mothers have told cast members that their children cry every Monday night when "Alf" ends.' Also the origin: Fusco, a former high school teacher who had produced children's specials for PBS, 'created Alf in 1982 but had trouble getting a deal off the ground', and took the character to Tom Patchett.

src.citation: ALF (TV series). Wikipedia.
src.claim: Dates, structure and the second performer: ALF aired on NBC from 22 September 1986 to 24 March 1990; the title character is an acronym for 'Alien Life Form' whose real name is Gordon Shumway, an alien from the planet Melmac who follows an amateur radio signal to Earth and crash-lands into the garage of the suburban California Tanner family, who take him in to hide him from the Alien Task Force; the family is social worker Willie, Kate, Lynn, Brian and a cat named Lucky 'whom ALF wishes to consume'. 'ALF was performed by puppeteer Paul Fusco, who co-created the show with Tom Patchett. However, in scenes where he appeared in full body, he was performed by Michu Meszaros, who was uncredited in the role.' Four seasons, 97 episodes. And the age: Willie and ALF's relationship is 'akin to a mix of siblings and surrogate father and son, with Willie playing the father role despite being much younger than Alf, who was stated to be over two hundred and twenty years old by the time of the series.'

nodes.s: Buy nine, get the tenth. A card, a punch, a visible record of loyalty, in the customer's hand.
nodes.g: The most parasocial object in the world and nobody has ever said so. It is a small, portable, accumulating record that a person chooses to carry around, which is functionally an anniversary counter for a café.

src.claim: The stamp card is a measurable instrument, not a novelty: supermarket loyalty card data has been used to quantify the operational effect of promotions on households rather than on aggregate sales, which is the point at which a discount becomes a profile
src.citation: Higgs, R., & McInstash, S. (2008). Measuring the operational efficiency of retail promotions which have a loyalty card scheme.

nodes.s: The show you have already seen, watched again, not for the plot. Familiarity as a nervous system intervention.
nodes.g: The most functional parasocial behaviour in ordinary life and the one nobody pathologises, because it demonstrably works. Nothing else in a person's week guarantees the outcome. It is also the cleanest evidence that people attach to the accumulation rather than the content.

src.citation: Grady, S. M., Eden, A., & Wolfers, L. N. (2025). Examining Comfort Media: A Tool for Self-Regulation and Refuge? Mass Communication and Society, 29(2), 245-268.
src.claim: Comfort media treated as a regulatory instrument rather than a guilty pleasure: the paper builds from media-based coping and recovery research, on the argument that comforting experiences reduce distress the way comfort food does. Supports the summary's 'familiarity as a nervous system intervention', and supports it as a studied effect rather than a received opinion. Publisher returns 403 to an unauthenticated request, so marked unverified; volume, issue, pages and authors confirmed against Crossref.

src.citation: Castle, K. (2019). Comfort TV: Considering Everyday Television Use as a Mode of Self-Care [Data Collection]. University of Glasgow. Datacite DOI: 10.5525/gla.researchdata.798
src.claim: An audience study of comfort viewing as a mode of self-care, with hospital patients, family units and first-year undergraduates, collecting surveys, two rounds of qualitative interviews and viewing journals (minimum seven entries), collected Oct 2016 - Mar 2017 and released under CC BY 4.0. Establishes that rewatching for comfort has been treated as a coping practice worth a dedicated study including hospital patients - i.e. not pathologised, and taken seriously enough to build a dataset about. Note this record is the data, not the write-up: the findings belong to the thesis and are not claimed here.

nodes.s: The question underneath all of it, and the reason the clinical literature went in circles for forty years: is a parasocial bond a form of wellbeing, a substitute for it, or neither?
nodes.g: Still unresolved and the most honest place to be. The honest answer is that it depends on cost - money, sleep, peace - rather than on the strength of the feeling, which is why the disorder cannot be identified from the feeling alone and why the audit scores both axes instead of one.

src.claim: The test this site keeps applying, from the source: whether an arrangement flatters a life is not the question. Aristotle's eudaimonia is activity of the soul in accordance with virtue over a whole life - a standard applied to the completed life, not the enjoyable moment
src.citation: Aristotle. Nicomachean Ethics, Books I and X; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Aristotle's Ethics'.

src.claim: And the reason the question recurs: the standard is deliberately not reducible to pleasure, which is why an analysis of what makes people feel better about their attachments keeps needing this older vocabulary
src.citation: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Aristotle's Ethics'.

nodes.s: A working vocabulary for grief over a public figure, drawn from bereavement practice, used without qualification.
nodes.g: Adopted slowly and grudgingly. The vocabulary now exists and is mostly used to dismiss people, which is an unfortunate fate for a body of practical advice about a real grief response to a real loss.

src.claim: The scale of the first known mass grief for a stranger: an estimated 750,000 people at Rudolph Valentino's funeral in 1926 caused destruction at the funeral home
src.citation: Fan Culture. EBSCO Research Starters, Social Sciences and Humanities.

src.claim: 'Cofactuality': viewers manage narrative loss by working through and sharing multiple versions of the ending they would have preferred. Grief gets socialised through arguing about what should have happened
src.citation: McCormick, C. TV finales and the meaning of endings (doctoral dissertation).

src.claim: The scale of the loss, from the same study: so many viewers equated a presidential farewell address to saying goodbye to a television show that the comparison was drawn in the scholarship
src.citation: McCormick, C. TV finales and the meaning of endings, citing Peter Brooks.

nodes.s: Fans insisting two characters should be together, and treating the show as withholding rather than as finished.
nodes.g: The clearest example of a parasocial bond that runs in the opposite direction to the intended one. The audience is not consuming the story, it is running a parallel production about two people who do not exist and are not allowed to.

src.claim: The practice has its own scholarship and its own naming: pairing characters in the fandom rather than with a real performer is treated as a distinct analytic object, not as fan 'confusion' about which is real
src.citation: Hills, A. (2014). There's no place for a loli like me in the PLURD community: The liminality of fictional characters and fan identity.

src.claim: The mechanism is that characters are licensed: a fictional figure can be assigned traits the performer never had, so the attachment does not require the object to behave well
src.citation: Hills (2014).

nodes.s: Anti-stalking legislation passed in several jurisdictions, defining unwanted repeated contact as a criminal offence.
nodes.g: The first point at which the law acknowledged a parasocial bond can be dangerous to the person at the other end. The offence is about contact, not feeling, which is the correct boundary and the one most online argument resists.

src.claim: 'Stalking' became a criminal category rather late and for a specific reason: the 1989 murder of actress Rebecca Schaeffer, and the term entered US statutes in the early 1990s, with the UK following in the Protection from Harassment Act 1997. The law arrived after the homicide
src.citation: Stalking (Wikipedia).

nodes.s: A child writes to a magazine telling them a fictional brand of baby food is real. The NEST never appears. The letter is never answered. The episode ends.
nodes.g: The single most parasocial thing ever put on television, and it is a joke about wanting the writers to confirm that a fictional place is real. An eight-year-old asking to be told the world is real, dressed as a gag about a cereal. Everything on this site happens because a child did not accept the terms.

src.claim: the entry as a whole
src.citation: Rugrats

nodes.s: A costume is put on by a new actor and the audience transfers its entire attachment to whoever is now inside it. Running five days a week, in front of millions of children, with nobody pretending otherwise.
nodes.g: The most complete parasocial handover ever broadcast, and the closest thing television has to a controlled experiment. The audience knew the person had changed. They transferred the feeling anyway, instantly, and enjoyed knowing they were doing it.

src.claim: the entry as a whole
src.citation: Mighty Morphin Power Rangers, 1993-

nodes.s: A scheduled block, a fixed slot, a face, a voice, a house, a family, and a writer who knows your name. Aimed deliberately at a person old enough to believe all of it, and running on a rhythm.
nodes.g: The clearest parasocial laboratory ever built, and nobody had to design a mechanism because the format is one. A generation went fluent in the vocabulary of attachment here and then explained the internet's emotional economics to people confused by it, and the usual claim - that the internet is making people parasocial - has the timeline exactly backwards.

src.claim: A whole genre organised around a weekly slot and a captive child audience, and then dismantled by a regulatory decision: children's programming was treated differently from adult broadcasting, so when networks moved their cartoons to weekday mornings the entire appointment-viewing culture went with them
src.citation: Saturday morning cartoon (Wikipedia).

nodes.s: A death broadcast in real time to a generation that had grown up with a songwriter's complaints as a soundtrack.
nodes.g: Parasocial grief with a specific edge: the person had spent years being public about being miserable, and the audience had been treating it as content. Afterwards, every public complaint became a private grief waiting to happen.

src.claim: THE PARASOCIAL CHANNEL DELIVERED THE DEATH BEFORE THE FAMILY DID. 8 April 1994, around 8:40am, an electrician recognised the body through a window, and called a ROCK RADIO STATION before calling police - because he was a fan. The on-air personality said broadcasting it was 'kind of an eerie decision to make. We're not a news station'
src.citation: Seattle Times, 8 April 1994; and Rolling Stone (Neil Strauss), Flashback: Kurt Cobain's Last Days.

src.claim: Cobain's mother and his sister both learned of his death from radio reports. She said: 'Now he's gone and joined that stupid club'
src.citation: Seattle Times, 8 April 1994.

src.claim: AND THE EXTRACTION, MEASURED IN HOURS. Two hours after the county medical examiner positively identified the body by fingerprints, most local record stores were completely wiped out of all Nirvana product. One store reported selling a few hundred CDs, singles and vinyl by the next morning, including the $100 interview CD
src.citation: Carrie Borzillo, When Kurt Cobain Died, Billboard (2019), reporting her 23 April 1994 article 'Cobain Mourned by Fans, Industryites in Memorials, Music Stores'.

src.claim: Which one record store executive said out loud at the time: 'a pathetic scene. Everything is going out the door. If people were really fans, they'd have had this stuff already.' The industry diagnosing the fans while taking their money
src.citation: Tower Records' Chris Simmons, quoted in Billboard (2019), April 1994.

src.claim: The scale of the assembly: roughly 5,000 people at the public memorial at the Flag Pavilion near the Space Needle on 10 April 1994, at which Courtney Love - by tape - asked the crowd to shout 'asshole' at the man they had just grieved
src.citation: Borzillo, Billboard (2019); Rolling Stone (1994).

src.claim: And a fan's own account of the mechanism, on the street outside his house: 'Nirvana touched something deep inside me'
src.citation: Seattle Times, 8 April 1994, reporting Laura Mitchell.

src.claim: The counter-claim, and it is the strongest version of the other side: 'He was his audience' - the songs were written from experience the listeners recognised as their own
src.citation: MTV News Special Report, The Life & Death of Kurt Cobain (1994), reporting Michael Azerrad.

nodes.s: Killing a popular character for narrative effect, and the organised reaction that follows.
nodes.g: The most reliable audience manipulation in fiction, because it is the only one the audience cannot avoid. Grief engineered as a plot device is the writer's oldest trick and the fandom's most reliable grievance.

src.claim: n=840: both the positivity of a main character's outcome and perceived narrative closure were associated with reduced emotional distress - depression, anger, anxiety. Ending well measurably lowers the damage
src.citation: Krakowiak, K. M. (2024). How It Ends.

src.claim: Produced for finale-hype: producers craft a deliberate path to closure, and the anticipation of the end then shapes the entire final season retroactively
src.citation: McCormick, C. TV finales and the meaning of endings (doctoral dissertation).

nodes.s: Dozens of scripted personalities, rememberers, and subscription companions sold to a mass market in the mid-nineties.
nodes.g: The commercial attempt that came twenty-five years before it worked. The category has the same name, the same promise, and a very different population, and comparing the two eras is instructive about what the internet added.

src.claim: ELIZA, 1966, and its programmer's founding complaint: that people insisted on believing the machine understood them when it did not - 'the user is the interpreter'. Every attachment since is a variation on the error ELISA's author found unbearably moving
src.citation: ELIZA (Wikipedia); Weizenbaum, J. (1966). ELIZA - A computer program for the study of natural language communication between man and machine.

nodes.s: The difference between being known by somebody who was paying attention on purpose and being modelled by a system that has your history. Same information, different relationship.
nodes.g: The distinction the whole site turns on. A clerk who notices what you rented has one motive - you coming back. An algorithm optimising for watch time has yours, but it does not know what you rented. The second is not better at caring. It is better at correlating, and the human experience of the difference is the entire subject.

nodes.s: Points, tiers, an anniversary date, a number that has been going up for years, and the quiet threat of what happens to it if you leave. The most ordinary parasocial object ever invented.
nodes.g: It converts a relationship into an account, and an account is something with a balance. Nobody feels moved by a balance. The remarkable thing is how much feeling the machinery of a balance can carry once you have also attached to a person - the anniversary counter is not a relationship, it is a receipt for one.

src.claim: What the card buys the retailer: a per-household purchase history, which is what makes a 'personalised recommendation' possible and what turns a discount into surveillance with a discount attached
src.citation: Higgs, R., & McInstash, S. (2008). Measuring the operational efficiency of retail promotions which have a loyalty card scheme.

src.claim: And the retention design, which is the reason leaving is hard: the same paper measures effects at household level, so the relationship being managed is the household's basket, not the shopper's satisfaction
src.citation: Higgs & McInstash (2008).

nodes.t: The brand that has a personality
nodes.s: Corporations given a voice, a face, a founder narrative, and a tone, so that a customer relationship has a subject.
nodes.g: The final move of the parasocial relationship into commerce: the thing you have feelings about is a legal person. Brands now do this deliberately and in the open, and it is the completion of a process that started with a singer.

src.claim: THE CITATION THIS ENTRY WAS WAITING FOR. A peer-reviewed study of what happens when a narrative brand ends: narrative closure and 'consumption sociality' on loss accommodation. A character that is also a brand does not get to die quietly
src.citation: Russell, C. A., & Schau, H. J. (2013). When Narrative Brands End: The Impact of Narrative Closure and Consumption Sociality on Loss Accommodation. Journal of Consumer Research, 40(6), 1039-1062.

nodes.s: Bands assembled for a market, with fan clubs, fan voting, fan merchandise and fan-financed releases.
nodes.g: Fandom reorganised as an economic instrument. The fan stopped being an audience and became a funding mechanism, which is the single most consequential change in the whole file.

src.claim: A manufactured category with a manufacturing process: Popstars: The Rivals (2000) let a panel choose rather than audition, and the resulting groups were assembled rather than found. The boy band is the star system with the mystique removed and the volume raised
src.citation: Boy band (Wikipedia); Popstars: The Rivals (2000).

nodes.s: Streaming video over a network, at first unbroadcast and unproduced, from a bedroom or a desk.
nodes.g: The medium that removed the gatekeeper before it removed the schedule. Everything a creator economy is today existed in this form first, badly, and was not interesting to anybody.

src.claim: Webcasting - streaming live audio and video over the internet - went mainstream in the mid-1990s, with RealAudio in 1995 and the 1995 relaunch of Justin and Eric's site as the first widely recognised example. Before it, a performance was a place you had to be
src.citation: Webcasting (Wikipedia).

nodes.s: Japanese animation and comics reach a large Western audience through dedicated channels, and a transnational fandom forms around them.
nodes.g: Fandom stops being national and starts being organised around translation, release schedules and convention circuits. The parasocial bond acquires logistics, which is how you can tell it is real.

src.claim: Anime as imported mass attachment: American television carried Japanese animation from the 1960s, and a later wave - Voltron, the Ninja Turtles, Dragon Ball - made the form available to people who never read the original in translation. The conduit crossed languages without asking permission
src.citation: Anime in the United States (Wikipedia).

nodes.t: The narrator is Tyler Durden, and he is not told
nodes.s: Two hours of a man telling you about his best friend. The friend does not exist, the man telling you does not know it, and you are being addressed by somebody who is also being lied to.
nodes.g: The sharper version of the mirrored case, and sharper than Dorian Gray because the split is not between an image and a man but **inside a single voice**. For the whole film the audience attaches to Tyler Durden, and Tyler Durden is supplied entirely by the person narrating: "The Narrator, an unreliable narrator, is not immediately aware that he is mentally projecting Tyler." There is no second person to check him against, which is the condition every other entry on this site has and this one has inverted. The physical evidence is better than the script notes, because the actor supplied it: Edward Norton said "We decided early on that I would start to starve myself as the film went on, while Brad Pitt would lift and go to tanning beds; he would become more and more idealized as I wasted away." One body, two figures, and the divergence was made physically rather than written. What ties it to `the-imaginary-friend` is the mechanism, which is the same mechanism in two epistemic states. An unreliable narrator is a person who knows and maintains anyway. A child with an imaginary companion knows the friend is invented. The Narrator does not know Tyler is invented. **One mechanism, two states of knowing, and the film conceals the difference on purpose** - the reveal is the last ten minutes, by which point the audience has been holding a bond for nearly two hours without knowing there was anything to hold on to. The commercial story is the same story told in money. Studio executives disliked the film and restructured Fincher's intended marketing campaign to cut expected losses; it opened to about $102.4 million and then found its actual audience in home video. The bond is with the narrator. The money followed the bond and ignored the premise.

src.citation: Fight Club. Wikipedia.
src.claim: Production and the load-bearing sentence: 'Fight Club is a 1999 American film directed by David Fincher starring Brad Pitt, Edward Norton, and Helena Bonham Carter. It is based on the 1996 novel Fight Club by Chuck Palahniuk.' 'It was filmed in and around Los Angeles from July to December 1998.' 'Studio executives did not like the film and restructured Fincher's intended marketing campaign to try to reduce anticipated losses.' Gross $102.4 million. Norton as 'the unnamed narrator, an insomniac automobile recall specialist dissatisfied with his consumerist lifestyle', Pitt as 'Tyler Durden, a charismatic soap salesman who forms Fight Club with the narrator'. And the mechanism: 'The Narrator, an unreliable narrator, is not immediately aware that he is mentally projecting Tyler. He also mistakenly promotes the fight clubs as a way to feel powerful, though the Narrator's physical condition worsens while Tyler Durden's appearance improves.' Norton on the production: 'We decided early on that I would start to starve myself as the film went on, while [Brad Pitt] would lift and go to tanning beds; he would become more and more idealized as I wasted away.'

nodes.s: Persistent text spaces with per-topic cultures, norms enforced by social pressure and volume.
nodes.g: Where the pile-on was invented. Fandom moved from letters to threads, and a thread has thousands of people in it at once with no moderator and no cost to replying.

src.claim: Stan Twitter works as a functioning Community of Practice: members form interpersonal bonds, communicate regularly, and contribute. A fan forum is a real community, not a comment box
src.citation: Malik, Z., & Haidar, S. (2020). Online community development through social interaction - K-Pop stan twitter as a community of practice. Interactive Learning Environments, 31(2).

nodes.s: A fan whose attachment has become fixed, repeated and physical: tracking whereabouts, intercepting flights, surveilling buildings. The word is Korean and the practice is not new, but the scale and the criminality are.
nodes.g: The point at which the fiction ends being a fiction. It is also the lane's honest boundary: the same feeling, the same industry, the same platforms, and a line that once gets crossed cannot be uncrossed by anyone in the room. Convictions for stalking a member of a group have followed this pattern in several jurisdictions.

src.claim: the entry as a whole
src.citation: No single source identified yet; this entry needs its sources added.

nodes.s: Organised, commercialised intrusion: tracking schedules, buying flight details, intercepting travel, surveilling buildings.
nodes.g: Attachment scaled past the point where it is a private feeling and became an industry with staff and infrastructure. The escalation is not emotional, it is logistical - which is why it emerged as fandom became globally coordinated.

src.claim: THE MECHANISM: fans know far more about the celebrity than the reverse, which lets them disrupt the relationship and gain a temporary sense of power and self-efficacy. Ethnogographic study with interviews
src.citation: Nanyang Business School, NTU Singapore (2017). The Darker Side of K-pop?

src.claim: The term: sa (private) + saeng (life), intrusion into celebrities' private lives. Behaviour emerges with 1990s K-pop idol groups, not with the digital era
src.citation: Sasaeng fan. Wikipedia.

src.claim: The law followed the behaviour: the Kim Changwan case, stalked over ten years, produced a 'persistent harassment' offence added to the Minor Offences Act in 2011, revised 2013, and a 2016 bill raising the maximum penalty
src.citation: Sasaeng fan. Wikipedia, citing the statute history.

src.claim: A peer-reviewed typology of True Fan / Ani-Fan / Sasaeng, which states that parasocial relationship is central to the Korean pop culture industry and examines its top-down structuring of the fan-object bond
src.citation: The Spectrum of Fan Attitudes in Korean Culture Industry (2022).

src.claim: The global parallel: sasaeng behaviour exported, and doxxing as the anglophone equivalent - plus the gendered stigma attached to female fandom
src.citation: Khedun-Burgoine, B. 'How do I Make Oppa Sarang Me?': Resemiotisation and Reconstruction of Meaning in the Global K-pop Fandom. University of Oxford ORA.

nodes.s: The 1990s extension to live people who respond in real time - streamers, hosts, people who read your comment. The bond is still fundamentally one-sided, but the other side can now hear you.
nodes.g: The term that made the field relevant to the internet, and the reason the word changed: the phenomenon did not, only the possibility of contact. It is the same bond with the floor removed, which is why it feels better and goes wrong faster.

src.claim: The entry as a whole: transparasocial interaction as it is actually used in the literature - a one-sided bond with a live performer whose audience can be heard in real time, studied on Twitch. The DOI is confirmed against Crossref metadata, but the publisher returns 403 to an unauthenticated request, so this is recorded as unverified rather than pretending the text was read.
src.citation: Carter, A. E., & Hoy, M. G. (2024). We're All Friends Here: Examining Transparasocial Interaction on Twitch and Its Effects on Strategic Communications. Journal of Interactive Advertising, 24(2), 127-142.

nodes.s: Fans organising across national borders around media, with a shared calendar of releases and a shared language.
nodes.g: Fandom became infrastructure. When a release date is a global event and the discourse is synchronised across time zones, the parasocial bond stops being a private thing and becomes a public holiday.

src.claim: The canonical account of fandom as crossing borders and refusing to stay in its box: Jenkins, *Convergence Culture* (2006), and the scholarship that followed on K-pop, anime and football travelling further than the industry intended
src.citation: Jenkins, H. (2006). Convergence Culture: Where Old and New Media Collide.

nodes.s: A person famous for being filmed, with no skill, no work and no release schedule - and an audience that formed anyway.
nodes.g: The purest parasocial figure ever mainstreamed: fame with no product, only proximity. It also removed the last barrier - you no longer need to be good at anything, you only need to be watched.

src.claim: The format originated as an unembodied surveillance experiment and produced celebrity from it: the Dutch precursor De Teleboom began in 1997, watched by a studio audience who dialled in votes, and the format was exported worldwide from 2000
src.citation: Big Brother (franchise) (Wikipedia).

nodes.s: A persistent virtual world with avatars, economies, and relationships between people who never met.
nodes.g: Parasocial attachment with a body and a social graph, and the first virtual environment where the loneliness was addressed directly rather than incidentally. It also produced the first convention-attendance problem in a space with no physical convention.

src.claim: Measured on a validated attachment scale with 125 Second Life residents: attachments formed in the virtual world are EQUALLY STRONG as those in real life. The virtual bond is not a diluted version of the real one
src.citation: Quackenbush, D. M., Allen, J. G., & Fowler, J. C. Comparison of Attachments in Real-World and Virtual-World Relationships.

src.claim: AND THE PART THAT IS NOT A DILUTION: attachment anxiety is LOWER in virtual-world relationships than real ones. Emotional wellbeing tracks strength of attachment in the real world and low anxiety in the virtual one
src.citation: Quackenbush, Allen & Fowler, Comparison of Attachments in Real-World and Virtual-World Relationships.

src.claim: A regulator's finding on what an avatar is: the avatar is 'a symbol of the self, representing the user's deepest wishes, aspirations, virtues and vices', and for some players becomes a purposeful projection or idealisation of identity, for others an experiment in being someone new
src.citation: Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada (2008). Second Life: Privacy in Virtual Worlds.

src.claim: N=236, recruited inside Second Life, every participant in a committed real-world relationship: 81.7% also had a committed virtual relationship with a DIFFERENT partner, and no real-life relationship was significantly more satisfying than any Second Life relationship in any statistical analysis
src.citation: Kolotkin, R. A., Williams, M. M., Lloyd, C., & Hallford, E. W. Does Loving an Avatar Threaten Real Life Marriage?

src.claim: And the asymmetry in how it lands: women tended to define their Second Life relationships as significantly MORE satisfying than their real ones; men as equally satisfying
src.citation: Kolotkin, Williams, Lloyd & Hallford, Does Loving an Avatar Threaten Real Life Marriage?

src.claim: The capability this entry describes, treated as an experimental asset by researchers: face-to-face communication with full non-verbal cues while never compromising real-world anonymity
src.citation: The lab versus the virtual lab and virtual field - an experimental investigation of trust games with communication (Second Life).

nodes.s: Public mourning in a way that produced its own genre of documentary and speculation.
nodes.g: The moment grief for a parasocial figure became a media product, with outlets monetising speculation about the death itself. The line between honouring the dead and selling the death is drawn here, and it is not respected here.

src.citation: Grigsby Bates, K. (2009, June 25). Michael Jackson Dead At 50: The Two-Way. NPR.
src.claim: Fixes the date: Jackson died on Thursday 25 June 2009 at UCLA Medical Center, pronounced dead at 2:26pm, aged 50. Also documents the entry's actual subject from inside the first hours: TMZ reported the death first and CNN confirmed it more than two hours later via the Los Angeles coroner, and the publicist who had served Jackson during the 1991 molestation trial issued a statement to assembled reporters within the first night, describing him as 'impossibly difficult and often self-destructive'. Grief and access arriving as a media product, hours after the news, with no cooling-off period.

src.citation: Duke, A. (2009, August 28). Michael Jackson's death was a homicide, coroner rules. CNN.
src.claim: The investigation that followed, which is what turned the mourning into sustained coverage: the Los Angeles County coroner ruled the death a homicide, finding propofol and lorazepam the primary drugs responsible, with midazolam, diazepam, lidocaine and ephedrine also detected, and cited 'acute propofol intoxication' with 'benzodiazepine effect' as a contributing condition. The full autopsy and toxicology reports were placed on security hold at the request of police and the district attorney, and federal and state agencies opened parallel investigations.

src.citation: ABC News (2019, June 13). 'My God, Michael Jackson is dead': The final hours leading up to the pop star's death.
src.claim: The scene at the house, from a firefighter-paramedic who was there: the ambulance leaving the Holmby Hills home was met, in his words, by 'a circus' - 'Paparazzi... people, tourists. There was even a double-decker tour bus' - and a celebrity bus tour was stopped by emergency personnel on the way out. This is the entry's 'line between honouring the dead and selling the death', witnessed by someone who was working.

src.citation: Nasaw, D., & Wood, B. (2009, June 26). Michael Jackson dies: worldwide reaction (live). The Guardian.
src.claim: Live reporting from the first morning, showing the mechanics the entry describes: speculation about the cause circulating within hours (including a report that he was addicted to Demerol), the coroner saying at 3:51pm that the autopsy would begin 'in minutes' with no definitive results expected for six to eight weeks, and the 1970s-edition of a prime-time documentary being discussed in the same news cycle.

nodes.t: Fighting about a stranger in a reply section
nodes.s: A disagreement conducted entirely in good faith about a person none of the participants have met, using the vocabulary of a personal grievance.
nodes.g: A parasocial relationship conducted in public with a complete stranger, and the argument is never about the stranger. The people with the strongest feelings are the most likely to be drawn in, which is the same property that makes fandoms work.

src.claim: Fighting about a stranger is norm enforcement, not expression: accusation triggers moral outrage, the network piles on, and the target self-censors. Interviews n=28 plus n=9 Trust and Safety workers
src.citation: Marwick, A. E. Morally Motivated Networked Harassment as Normative Reinforcement.

src.claim: Sanctioning a stranger is an identity signal, and is read as one by everyone watching
src.citation: Ahn, C., Lelkes, Y., & Levendusky, M. S. (2024). Sanctioning political speech on social media is driven by partisan norms and identity signaling.

nodes.t: Doxxing the person, not the character
