nodes.s: The jump from disliking a fictional portrayal to locating and publishing a real person's address. The word had to be invented for a grievance that used to be settled by writing a letter.
nodes.g: The escalation everyone predicted and nobody predicted the timing of. Note what the parasocial frame does here: the audience is not attached to the person being targeted, they are attached to somebody playing them. The harm lands on a human who did not choose to be a character.

src.claim: Organised exposure of personal information used as a campaign tactic rather than incidental doxxing, documented as a distinct practice and separately criminalised in a number of jurisdictions
src.citation: Doxxing (Wikipedia).

nodes.s: Fans are injured or killed attempting to get closer to a performer, in volume, repeatedly, for years.
nodes.g: Direct physical risk from proximity-seeking, and the clearest line where attachment stops being a private matter and becomes somebody else's liability.

src.claim: 5 November 2021, Astroworld, Houston: ten deaths in a crowd crush, with the fatal bottleneck forming while attendees were still recording and posting to social media from inside it. The audience was filming the audience being injured
src.citation: Astroworld Festival (Wikipedia).

nodes.t: The character is not the person
nodes.s: The pattern of locating and publishing a private address over a disliked fictional portrayal.
nodes.g: Escalation past the point of no return, and the reason the whole lane needs to exist rather than being left off the site as uncomfortable. The public is not attached to the person being targeted, which is the detail that makes it indefensible.

src.claim: Doxxing and public shaming are the standard repertoire of morally motivated networked harassment (n=28 targets, n=9 platform Trust and Safety staff)
src.citation: Marwick, A. E. Morally Motivated Networked Harassment as Normative Reinforcement.

src.claim: People judge harassment MORE justified and more deserved - though not more appropriate - when the target has done something. Retribution drives it (n=160, n=432)
src.citation: Blackwell, L., Chen, T., Schoenebeck, S., & Lampe, C. When Online Harassment Is Perceived as Justified. ICWSM.

nodes.s: When a service ends or changes, the company sends an apology, sometimes with credit, addressed personally.
nodes.g: A corporation performing grief at its own users, correctly, because the users are grieving. The apology is not insincere and the technique is nonetheless the most sophisticated parasocial manipulation on this page, and it is free.

src.citation: Gross, D. (2013, March 14). Google Reader shutting down on July 1. CNN Business.
src.claim: The mechanism, its vocabulary, and the detail the entry's argument depends on. Google's line: 'We know Reader has a devoted following who will be very sad to see it go. We're sad too.' Within hours more than 46,000 people had signed a Change.org petition, and its author stated the entry's thesis outright: 'This isn't just about our data in Reader. This is about us using your product because we love it, because it makes our lives better, and because we trust you not to nuke it.' And the commercial fact underneath it: 'The feeds are also difficult to make money from, and Google never tried to place ads on Reader or charge for its use.'

src.citation: Rothman, J. (2013, March 15). Farewell, Dear Reader. The New Yanker's Page-Turner.
src.claim: The grief, and its object. A user describes Reader as the first site he saw each morning and the last before bed, likens losing it to a favourite old bookshop closing, and then locates the real loss precisely: 'I won't miss Reader when it shuts down. But I will miss the old me - the person I described in Google Reader, without knowing it.' Which is this site's grief entry turned inside out: what was mourned was not the company but a version of the person who had used it.

src.citation: Sottek, T. (2013, March 13). Google Closes The Book On Google Reader On July 1. TechCrunch.
src.claim: The service's own send-off and the reason given: Reader launched in 2005, would be retired on 1 July 2013, and Google told users 'Thanks for 8 great years!' - which is where this entry's 2005 date comes from. Usage had declined while other services were cut in the same spring cleaning, and Reader had been left without significant updates.

nodes.s: Uploads become trivially cheap and the audience begins to attach to individuals rather than channels.
nodes.g: Attachment shifts from institutions to people at exactly the point the distribution cost goes to zero. The broadcaster's ten-year relationship with a channel becomes a viewer's ten-year relationship with a face.

src.claim: Founded 14 February 2005 as a side project by four people, one of whom later described it as a hobby with the feature set of a TV channel. The first upload was 'Me at the zoo'; it passed a million users by the end of 2005
src.citation: YouTube (Wikipedia).

nodes.s: Roughly half a billion phone numbers become dialable, a fan can in principle hear a recorded voice, and the novelty ringtone sells the idea that a performer can be present in a pocket for about four years.
nodes.g: The real discontinuity, and a much narrower one than the standard story. The feeling was not new; the possibility of contact was. The reply is now structurally impossible in a way a letter never was - an email is not paper, it does not have to be opened, and the person reading it has a thousand. The conditions that made a reply work were small enough for one human to hold, and they are gone permanently.

src.claim: THE PHONE AS A PERSON, MEASURED. Idol messaging apps are described in the literature as simulating parasocial interaction by allowing one-to-one texting with a performer, deepening the 'intensification' stage of attachment. Every user who used one said it increased their sense of connection
src.citation: The Psychological Impact of Parasocial Relationships on Adolescent K-pop Fans, citing Aw & Chua (2021), Kim & Song (2016), Bond (2016).

src.claim: Verbatim, from a 14-18 year old: 'It (Weverse) makes me feel like I'm talking to one of my best friends.' That is the whole entry, said by someone who had no vocabulary for it
src.citation: The Psychological Impact of Parasocial Relationships on Adolescent K-pop Fans.

nodes.s: Enforcement by volume: a position is declared untenable, a pile of people makes it so, and the outcome is a fact nobody chose.
nodes.g: Governance without authority. There is no court, no evidence standard and no appeal, only a critical mass of people who can agree, and the person on the losing end has the same parasocial attachment as everyone else and is treated as the problem.

src.claim: The mechanism: people are reluctant to be the FIRST to sanction anyone, but pile on once others have acted. Three experiments.
src.citation: Ahn, C., Lelkes, Y., & Levendusky, M. S. (2024). Sanctioning political speech on social media is driven by partisan norms and identity signaling.

src.claim: Pile-ons are learned, not spontaneous: positive social feedback for outrage raises future outrage, and users conform to their network's expressive norm
src.citation: Brady, N., et al. (2021). How social learning amplifies moral outrage expression in online social networks. Science Advances, 7(28), eabe5641.

src.claim: The outrage-mob shape, stated plainly: a few condemn, then more pile on with little regard for evidence (n=10,343)
src.citation: How reputation does (and does not) drive people to punish without looking. (2023).

nodes.s: An actor's persona and a character's persona are widely treated as the same thing, and one retires while the other continues.
nodes.g: The cleanest test of whether a parasocial bond attaches to a person or a role, and the answer changes depending on who is asked. The character outlives the actor, which is evidence for the fiction and against the man.

src.citation: Frye, J. (2013, May 3). Iron Man Unmasked: Robert Downey Jr., Don Cheadle & More Talk Character. The Credits, Motion Picture Association of America. (Courtesy of the Walt Disney Company.)
src.claim: The entry's question asked directly of the people who made the thing, rather than inferred from fan behaviour. Kevin Feige: 'How do you take a billionaire, industrialist playboy and make him relatable and somebody that you can root for?' and, on the alternative, 'take everything away from the character, which then makes you root for the guy'. Stephen Broussard on the boundary itself: even though the world knows and loves Tony Stark, 'he is still learning and struggling to define where Iron Man ends and his own life begins'. The unresolvable seam between persona and persona is named here by the people controlling it.

nodes.s: A performer with no media infrastructure becomes a global star through a video-sharing platform alone.
nodes.g: The first and clearest demonstration that a parasocial bond could be formed and monetised with no gatekeeper whatsoever. The platform was fourteen years old and the attachment was five.

src.citation: Justin Bieber Fast Facts. CNN.
src.claim: The sequence, which is three gatekeepers rather than none. 2007-2008: 'Bieber's mother begins posting videos of her son performing on YouTube. Record executive Scooter Braun sees the videos and flies Bieber and his mother to Atlanta and signs the teen to a contract.' 2008: auditions for Usher and is signed to Island/Def Jam. May 2009: 'One Time'. November 2009: the My World EP. Also the detail the entry was missing: in November 2009 an appearance at Roosevelt Field Mall in New York 'must be canceled due to an out-of-control crowd of teen girls' - a parasocial mass event inside the entry's own year, rather than a chart position.

src.citation: Adib, D. (2009, November 14). Pop Star Justin Bieber Is on the Brink of Superstardom. ABC News.
src.claim: Bieber's own account of the discovery layer, and the part that bypassed it: posting homemade covers from the age of twelve, 'It had a hundred views, then a thousand views, then ten thousand views, so I just kept posting more videos and more videos'. The piece also makes the chain explicit by comparison - 'Usher had "Star Search" to launch him out of obscurity at age 13. His new protege, Justin Bieber, had YouTube' - and records a bidding war, with Timberlake also interested before Usher won him for Island Def Jam.

nodes.s: The shift from selling things to selling attention, which means the commodity being bought is a person's feeling - and the seller is whoever is on the other end of it.
nodes.g: It gives the parasocial question its economic form. Once attention is the product, the parasocial bond is not a side effect of the business model, it is the business model. Every mechanism in the manipulation lane is a technique for converting affection into measurable minutes.

src.claim: the entry as a whole
src.citation: Wu, T. (2016). The Attention Merchants.

nodes.t: The dark pattern in the loyalty card
nodes.s: Exploiting the sunk cost of an earned balance: expiry, devaluation, tier demotion, and the deliberate design of loss.
nodes.g: Everything the field calls manipulation, expressed in the vocabulary of retail. The expiry date on a points balance is a grief event with a date on it, and it is engineered to occur annually.

src.claim: THE SUNK COST FALLACY, NAMED AS A DESIGN TECHNIQUE. 'Hidden Costs' reveals new charges immediately before purchase; the paper states this exploits the sunk cost fallacy - users feel so invested they justify the extra charge to avoid wasting their effort. The loyalty card is this
src.citation: Mathur, A., Acar, G., Friedman, M. J., Lucherini, E., Mayer, J., Chetty, M., & Narayanan, A. (2019). Dark Patterns at Scale: Findings from a Crawl of 11K Shopping Websites. Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction, 3(CSCW), Article 81.

src.claim: The asymmetry, stated as a category: it is easy to sign up for recurring subscriptions and memberships, but hard to cancel. 'Hard to Cancel' found on 31 websites
src.citation: Mathur et al. (2019), citing Gray et al. (2018) taxonomy; pattern originally Brignull's Roach Motel.

src.claim: Scale, and the part that indicts the industry: 1,818 dark pattern instances across 15 types and 7 categories on 1,254 of ~11,000 shopping websites (11.1%), with 234 instances on 183 websites exhibiting deceptive behaviour. More popular sites were MORE likely to feature them. And 22 third-party entities sell dark patterns as a turnkey solution
src.citation: Mathur et al. (2019). Dark Patterns at Scale.

src.claim: How hard: unsubscribing from Bloomberg took TEN clicks and required launching and conversing with a closed-domain chatbot first. Cancelling required entering first and last name into the chatbot welcome page, declining discount offers, answering a question to confirm, and completing a mandatory exit survey
src.citation: Staying at the Roach Motel: Cross-Country Analysis of Manipulative Subscription and Cancellation Flows (2024).

src.claim: Confirmation as a toll: The Daily Wire required a three-question mandatory survey AND typing the word 'CONFIRM' to cancel. The authors concede some friction prevents accidents, and note that requiring a typed phrase appears unnecessary
src.citation: Staying at the Roach Motel (2024).

src.claim: The harm is process harm: study of 53 Indian apps found 52 carried at least one deceptive pattern and e-commerce ran 5.3 per app against 2.7 across sectors, and argues the resulting regret is PROCESS regret from a bad decision procedure, not outcome regret from a bad product - which is why satisfaction metrics miss it
src.citation: Dark Patterns in Indian E-Commerce Interfaces and Consumer Purchase Regret. Research Review Journal of Social Science.

src.claim: It is now law, not preference: India's CCPA notified Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns on 30 November 2023, declaring thirteen practices unfair trade practices under the Consumer Protection Act 2019. The EU Digital Services Act uses the term 'dark patterns' officially
src.citation: Dark Patterns in Indian E-Commerce Interfaces and Consumer Purchase Regret, citing CCPA (2023) and DSA (2022).

nodes.s: Paid message apps where a window shaped exactly like the one holding your best friend costs about four dollars a month per artist, plus anniversary counters that make the bond feel cumulative and streaks that convert it into a hostage situation.
nodes.g: The lane where the feeling is genuine and the design is not accidental. Every mechanism here was tested, found to work, and shipped. The person is not being scammed, which is exactly what makes it difficult - the affection is real and so is the invoice, and the industry is extremely good at keeping those two facts in separate mental drawers.

src.claim: the entry as a whole
src.citation: No single source identified yet; this entry needs its series added.

nodes.s: The only intervention on this site that you do to yourself, and the only one nobody else can do for you. List your five strongest one-sided ties, score joy and cost, keep three, mute one, trade one hour a week toward a person in the room.
nodes.g: Not a cure and not a diagnostic. A rebalancing, done badly, about four times a year. It exists because the seventh law is the only part of the field that is actually yours, and because the numbers - one to ten, twice - make a feeling arguable.

nodes.s: Apparel, prints and objects released after a death, quickly, at a profit.
nodes.g: The commercial form of parasocial grief, and nobody involved pretends otherwise any more. It also sustains a cottage industry of people whose entire output is the deaths of people they never met.

src.claim: The commercial record of the immediate aftermath, in the trade press, in the same week: Billboard ran 'Cobain Mourned by Fans, Industryites in Memorials, Music Stores' on 23 April 1994 - memorials and merchandise as a single subject
src.citation: Borzen/Borzillo, Billboard (2019), reporting the 23 April 1994 article.

src.claim: And the deadline in which it must happen: within two hours of positive identification, the retail market for his work was empty. Grief merchandise has a shelf life measured in hours
src.citation: Borzillo, Billboard (2019).

nodes.s: The public performance of being at war with somebody, in public, for an audience, in a thread that never closes.
nodes.g: A parasocial relationship conducted with a second parasocial relationship attached - you are performing the fight for the room, not having it with the person. The room is the relationship and the person is the prop.

nodes.s: A monthly box of chosen items, an unboxing ritual, and a personal recommendation from somebody with taste.
nodes.g: The clerk behind a counter, automated and shipped monthly. The whole appeal is that a person chose this for you, and the whole trick is that the choice was made by a recommendation system.

src.claim: THE ENTRY'S MECHANISM, MEASURED. A controlled experiment (n=144) found unboxing COMPLEXITY has a main effect on positive affect (beta=.53, p=.020), and that positive affect in turn significantly increases willingness to share, online and off. The ritual is the product
src.citation: Berden, C. Thinking inside the box: the effect of the unboxing experience on positive affect and willingness to share (University of Twente MSc thesis).

src.claim: The scale of the ritual: an estimated 2.35 MILLION unboxing videos of the iPhone 6 were uploaded to YouTube in 2014, and about a quarter of a million were dedicated to a single subscription box brand. Unboxing became a genre with an audience
src.citation: Berden, Thinking inside the box, citing Bayston (2016).

src.claim: And it is treated as engineering, not whimsy: Apple designer Jonathan Ives on the practice - 'You design a ritual of unpacking to make the product feel special. Packaging can be theatre, it can create a story' - and the company tests hundreds of package designs in a dedicated unboxing room
src.citation: Berden, Thinking inside the box, citing Forbes (2014) and Mashable (2012).

src.claim: THE PART THAT IS ACTUALLY DISTURBING. An eye-tracking lab experiment found personalization improves the customer experience EVEN WHEN THE CUSTOMER DOES NOT PERCEIVE IT. Actual personalization shifts objective behaviour - attention concentrates on favoured products and they are more likely to be selected - while only perceived personalization moves subjective feelings
src.citation: Personalization and playful customer experience, with eye-tracking (Universite catholique de Louvain).

src.claim: The recommendation is the relationship: participants in a 2025 study emphasised the stylist or curator as the thing delivering the value, with algorithms used in the stylist's absence. Stylists keep notes, reference past purchases, and are trusted with items the subscriber says they would never have chosen
src.citation: Bhatt, D. (2025). Consumers' perceptions towards subscription retail: a focus on online fashion box services.

src.claim: And what participants named as the risks, unprompted: inability to opt out when not using the service, the time cost of interacting with a stylist, and the environmental cost of packaging and shipping. The convenience and the exit are the same design decision
src.citation: Bhatt (2025), citing Tao & Xu (2017).

src.claim: The shape of the relationship, named from 26 in-depth interviews: a subscription box journey has three stages - INITIATION, IMMERSION and EGRESS - each adding to or subtracting from utilitarian and hedonic value. Renewal and cancellation are stages of the same stream, not opposite decisions
src.citation: Alba, J. W. Navigating consumption streams: Toward a utilitarian-hedonic perspective on subscription box customer journeys. Journal of Consumer Behaviour.

nodes.s: The schedule goes from weekly to continuous and the bond loses its shape. A serial gives you a slot and a cliffhanger; an always-on feed has no slot and no gap to miss anybody in.
nodes.g: The rhythm was doing work nobody had measured. What replaced it is a permanent low-grade availability, which is a different emotional object: not a person who is more present, but one who is never finished, so there is no gap and therefore nothing to miss anybody in. The half of this the evidence supports is the gap - parasocial scales built in this period ask directly whether you miss characters when a show is between seasons, which is the thing an always-on feed removes. The other half it does not: where this entry's argument used to be that the bond loses its shape, the one controlled test of that mechanism found the bond getting *stronger*. Removing the slot does not obviously weaken the tie. It removes the absence, and the site has no evidence about what that costs.

src.citation: Erickson, S., Dal Cin, S., & Byl, H. (2019). An Experimental Examination of Binge Watching and Narrative Engagement. Social Sciences, 8(1), 19.
src.claim: Binge watching was experimentally manipulated, not merely correlated, and the reported result runs the OPPOSITE way to this entry's argument: it increased the strength of parasocial relationships and the intensity of narrative transportation. So the claim that the bond 'loses its shape' when the weekly rhythm is removed is this site's position, and the one controlled test of it found the bond getting stronger. Recorded rather than smoothed over. Publisher returns 403 to an unauthenticated request; authors, volume, issue and article number confirmed against Crossref.

src.citation: Anghelcev, G., Sar, S., Martin, J. D., & Moultrie, J. L. (2020). Binge-Watching Serial Video Content: Exploring the Subjective Phenomenology of the Binge-Watching Experience. Mass Communication and Society, 24(1), 130-154.
src.claim: Documents the gap at the centre of this entry as a measured thing rather than an impression: the parasocial scale items used include 'I miss my favorite characters when the show is on break between seasons', and the paper notes these bonds form in proportion to time spent with the characters. That is the missing-slot effect the summary describes - the thing a continuous feed removes is not the intensity but the absence. Publisher returns 403 to an unauthenticated request; bibliographic record confirmed against Crossref.

nodes.t: A mob is a parasocial event
nodes.s: Framing online harassment as a mob, and asking who is on it.
nodes.g: The most useful analytical frame available for a behaviour with no consequences for the people committing it, and the phrase that gets people to ask the question at all.

src.claim: THE PAPER'S OWN FRAMING IS THIS ENTRY. 'After an accusation of wrongdoing, an outrage mob appears. Initially, just a few condemn the accused. But before long, more and more people pile on, hastily meting out punishment with little regard for evidence or opposing perspectives.' Four studies, n=10,343
src.citation: Kteily, N., & Jordan, J. How reputation does (and does not) drive people to punish without looking.

src.claim: AND THE FINDING THAT CUTS AGAINST THE MORAL READING: there is NO reputational reward for not looking. Non-lookers were rated more loyal to the cause, but that was outweighed by a larger hit to perceived competence and fairness - evaluators rewarded punishers who LOOKED more generously
src.citation: Kteily & Jordan, How reputation does (and does not) drive people to punish without looking.

src.claim: The mechanism, named by the people in it: 'brigading, dogpiling, or calling out'. Amplification is the trigger - content moral-outrage spreads faster within like-minded networks, and 'drama' is consumed as entertainment in front of an audience
src.citation: Marwick, A. E. (2021). Morally Motivated Networked Harassment as Normative Reinforcement. Social Media Society, 7(2).

src.claim: What it actually achieves: harassment frequently results in the ACCUSED SELF-CENSORING, so the pile-on functions as a regulating force that removes speech from the public sphere. Neither platforms nor legal regulation protects against it. Interviews with 28 targets and 9 Trust and Safety workers
src.citation: Marwick, A. E. (2021). Social Media Society, 7(2).

src.claim: Not a partisan tactic, which is the part usually left out: this is used across the ideological spectrum, and the amplification runs in both directions depending on which network node shares it
src.citation: Marwick, A. E. (2021), Social Media Society, 7(2).

src.claim: WHY IT ESCALATES: analysis of 231 threads finds networked harassment runs in three phases - target introduction, network decision, network response - and that the crowd added narrative elements in at least 80% of threads, producing Continuous Narrative Escalation. The crowd is not reacting to the story. It is writing it
src.citation: Stoking the Flames: Understanding Escalation in an Online Harassment Community. Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction (2024).

src.claim: AND THE PART THAT MADE ME STOP: takedown requests are misused by the community and repurposed as ELEMENTS TO FURTHER FUEL THE NARRATIVE. Reporting abuse is itself harvested as content
src.citation: Stoking the Flames: Understanding Escalation in an Online Harassment Community (ACM CSCW 2024), analysis of 100 takedown request threads.

nodes.s: A voice assistant on every phone, addressing the user by name, knowing the user's calendar, and present in the home.
nodes.g: The crossover entry point. The assistant is not a celebrity and is not a friend, but it is a presence that knows you, and the relationship forms anyway and is categorised as neither friendship nor tool use.

src.claim: THE TITLE OF THE PAPER IS A PARTICIPANT'S SENTENCE. The study is titled 'I Almost Fell in Love with a Machine' after a subject's own private Instagram post about the conversational agent Lee. The authors state they did not expect any participant to develop a personal attachment
src.citation: Yu, Q., Nguyen, T., Prakkamakul, S., & Salehi, N. 'I Almost Fell in Love with a Machine': Speaking with Computers Affects Self-disclosure (UC Berkeley, X Lab).

src.claim: The mechanism, measured: people skipped FEWER invasive questions when listening and speaking than when reading and typing. It is the combination of both, not either alone, that triggers the social-actor response. The authors flag this as a new factor in user privacy concerns
src.citation: Yu, Nguyen, Prakkamakul & Salehi, 'I Almost Fell in Love with a Machine'.

src.claim: The warmth channel is where the work happens: emotional and opinion-based self-disclosure significantly increased perceived warmth over both normal conversation and factual disclosure, and high-intimacy disclosure fostered closer psychological connection, perceived empathy, friendliness and trustworthiness
src.citation: Sun, X., Shen, T., Jiang, Q., & Jiang, B. (2025). Research on the Impact of an AI Voice Assistant's Gender and Self-Disclosure Strategies.

src.claim: And why disclosure strategy has to be chosen rather than defaulted: research finds users who perceive an assistant as human-like form greater intimacy from PERSONAL disclosure, while users who perceive it as a machine form it from FACTUAL disclosure. The same utterance works only if you have already been read as a person
src.citation: Sun et al. (2025), citing Saffarizadeh et al. (2024).

src.claim: Gender is a dial on the conduit, not a decoration: a randomized experiment with 120 participants found a female voice produces higher perceived ANTHROPOMORPHISM, which in turn raises the credibility of the information it gives. Female voices also raised intended self-disclosure
src.citation: Do People Trust Female more than Male as a Voice Assistant? (Tampere University).

src.claim: The honest counterweight: warmth is the cheap channel and competence is not. Fiske et al. (2006) hold that warmth is the primary dimension while competence requires substantially more evidence to change - and disclosure strategy moved warmth but NOT competence. Reciprocal self-disclosure can also backfire entirely when users suspect manipulation, producing loss of trust, service cessation, and false answers in future disclosures
src.citation: Sun et al. (2025), citing Fiske et al. (2006) and Collins & Miller (1994).

nodes.s: Streaming gets a category, a vocabulary, a schedule, and a professional class of people who stream full time.
nodes.g: The first platform to treat a live one-sided relationship as a category worth designing for deliberately rather than tolerating incidentally.

src.claim: Twitch launched 6 June 2011 as a spin-off of Justin.tv's gaming section, named for 'twitch gameplay', in public beta
src.citation: Twitch (service). Wikipedia, citing contemporary coverage.

src.claim: The founder's own account of how a parasocial bond was accidentally engineered: an audio idea became a 24/7 camera feed following one person, then chat, then a community around watching
src.citation: Kan, J. (2011). Why Starting Justin.tv Was A Really Bad Idea, But I'm Glad We Did It Anyway. TechCrunch (guest post).

src.claim: Justin.tv began as Justin Kan broadcasting his life 24/7 from a cap-mounted camera at midnight on 19 March 2007 - the first and most parasocial thing on the platform
src.citation: Justin.tv. Wikipedia.

src.claim: Intimacy turned to intrusion almost immediately: viewers swatted Kan and sent large delivery orders to his apartment
src.citation: Justin.tv. Wikipedia, citing AllThingsD coverage of the TwitchTV launch.

src.claim: Contemporary launch coverage, 6 June 2011, E3 unveiling
src.citation: Duryee, T. (2011). Justin.tv Broadcasts Gamers' Every Move on TwitchTV. AllThingsD.

nodes.s: Organised conflict between fanbases, with brigading, ratioing and coalition behaviour, conducted with the grammar of war.
nodes.g: Fan organisations developed the same apparatus as states: recruitment, propaganda, alliance, denial. And the participants believe they are defending art.

src.claim: Documented case: the #fakewesteros Twitter community during the final season of Game of Thrones - fans of a character declared dead fighting fans who knew otherwise, over leaks
src.citation: Forcier, E. (2019). When the world ends: Study of #fakewesteros twitter fan community during the final season of Game of Thrones. Proceedings of the Association for Information Science and Technology, 56(1), 654-655.

src.claim: Fanwars are named by the fans themselves as the reason their own space is toxic - some avoid the app or deactivate their accounts rather than stay
src.citation: Ascue et al., Annyeong, Saranghae (De La Salle University).

nodes.s: Sending a false emergency report to a real address to provoke an armed police response, because of a grievance about a streamer.
nodes.g: The final boundary. A parasocial grievance aimed at a public figure lands on an innocent third party with a weapon, and no amount of the bond being sincere changes the outcome for the person who is shot.

src.claim: The term was coined in 2011 and the practice escalated from pranks to lethal: a 60-year-old man was killed in a swatting in California in 2013, after which California enacted specific anti-swattiing legislation. Armed police are dispatched as a joke with someone else's address attached
src.citation: Swatting (Wikipedia).

nodes.s: Coordinated harassment of women in games, disguised as a debate about whether harassment should be allowed.
nodes.g: The case study for how a parasocial grievance gets weaponised: people who felt strongly about a hobby organised against individuals who had done nothing personal to them. The counter is to ask who benefits from the fight, not what the disagreement is about.

src.claim: August 2014: a campaign targeting women in games, organised largely through an anonymous account, escalating within days to coordinated harassment, doxxing and death threats. The FBI investigated. Wikipedia's article is the de facto record and its revision history is itself an artifact of the harassment
src.citation: GamerGate (Wikipedia).

src.claim: The essay that started it was about the emotional labour of game design, which the campaign reframed as a grievance about women
src.citation: GamerGate (Wikipedia), discussing Begum Bayrak's 'Depression Quest' and Zoe Quinn.

nodes.t: The podcast as an intimate medium
nodes.s: A voice in your ear, unedited, twice a week, for years. The most parasocial habit in the English language and rarely discussed as such.
nodes.g: Nobody wears a costume and nobody mentions the format, so it never got examined. Researchers eventually measured it and found listeners score high on exactly the traits predicted: novelty-seeking, curiosity, and a need for good conversation.

src.claim: the entry as a whole
src.citation: Pedestrian.tv, 2026

nodes.s: A wave of studies measuring parasocial relationships with YouTubers, livestreamers and vloggers rather than with television hosts.
nodes.g: The literature caught up with the medium about a decade late, and then discovered that the newer bonds are not the same shape. Livestreamers can see the room. That changes the theory, not just the population.

src.claim: the entry as a whole
src.citation: Gerrath & Usrey, 2014

nodes.s: Evidence that the value of a celebrity endorsement falls when the audience suspects the relationship is a transaction.
nodes.g: The parasocial bond is doing the work, which means the suspicion destroys the asset. This is why an advert that says 'I love this' from somebody you follow is worth less than the same advert from a stranger: the transaction has to stay invisible.

src.claim: the entry as a whole
src.citation: de Vries & Gilovich, 2015

nodes.t: The people who are supposed to be reachable
nodes.s: Attachment to somebody we are not supposed to have feelings about: the teacher, the landlord, the local news anchor, the doctor's receptionist, the AI assistant that has read everything typed. The category no fandom site will admit exists.
nodes.g: The one that proves this is a hub rather than a fan site. The bond is identical in shape to the one with a celebrity and completely different in power, because here the other person does not know they are being related to and may have very little power to say no. It is also where my own classroom is, which is why it is an section and not a footnote.

src.claim: THE CATEGORY NO FANDOM SITE WILL ADMIT TO, demonstrated in a controlled experiment on people who were not asked to develop an attachment: one did, and said so publicly about the agent. Attachment to a machine is not a subculture. It is the default failure mode
src.citation: Yu, Nguyen, Prakkamakul & Salehi, 'I Almost Fell in Love with a Machine' (UC Berkeley, X Lab).

src.claim: Scale of what gets volunteered: on average participants skipped only 3 of 21 closeness-generating questions, responses were honest and conversational, most disclosed family life and values, some shared sensitive information, and one answered a question about their greatest accomplishment with 'Recovering from my mental illness'
src.citation: Yu, Nguyen, Prakkamakul & Salehi, 'I Almost Fell in Love with a Machine'.

src.claim: The category with the clearest evidence of failure: a real institution with a real constituency, using the full influencer apparatus, still cannot produce reciprocity. Priests seldom reply. The tie stays one-sided
src.citation: Between pulpit and platform: Parasocial bonds in Filipino priests' social media ministry (2025).

src.claim: And a counter-intuitive mechanism worth having: expressing positive feelings was the technique secular influencers rely on and the priests omitted, and the harvest step changed with it
src.citation: Witzel, The Cultivation and Harvesting of Parasocial Relationships for Evangelism.

nodes.s: A relationship with a competitor offered free while a subscription relationship is locked in behind the same login.
nodes.g: Platforms discovered that a user will defend the platform they have a relationship with against the platform offering them a better deal. The parasocial bond is now a competitive moat, and it is documented as such in the filings.

src.claim: The free trial as a documented pattern rather than an anecdote: Hidden Subscription is defined as charging a recurring fee under the pretense of a one-time fee or a free trial, and users often learn of it only days or months later
src.citation: Mathur, A., Acar, G., Friedman, M. J., Lucherini, E., Mayer, J., Chetty, M., & Narayanan, A. (2019). Dark Patterns at Scale. Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction, 3(CSCW), Article 81.

src.claim: And it is paired with a barrier on the way out: the same paper finds Hidden Subscription frequently co-occurs with Hard to Cancel, making the recurring charge harder to end than it was to begin
src.citation: Mathur et al. (2019).

nodes.s: A live stream with a visible comment feed, where the creator can read the room while the room watches itself. The first mass parasocial environment where the one-sided bond visibly, continuously, acknowledges you.
nodes.g: It solved a problem nobody had been able to solve: making the one-sided bond feel reciprocal without the labour of a real relationship. A creator glancing at your comment costs them nothing and lands like recognition. It is also the exact mechanism monetised two years later by the gifting economy.

src.claim: THE SITE'S THESIS, PUBLISHED: live streaming moves the parasocial relationship from one-sided to 'one-and-a-half sided', characterised by the potential for reciprocal communication, community affiliation and presence. Peer-reviewed, in a journal
src.citation: The one-and-a-half sided parasocial relationship. Current Opinion in Psychology.

src.claim: The bond persists through non-reciprocity: users keep following favourites despite failing to get a response - which is the whole subject, measured
src.citation: Crawford et al. (2020), cited in The one-and-a-half sided parasocial relationship.

src.claim: Merely WITNESSING the figure interact with other community members reinforces the viewer's connection - the bond forms on other people's exchanges, not on your own
src.citation: Stever & Lawson (2013), cited in The one-and-a-half sided parasocial relationship.

src.claim: Measured in the chat itself: streamer-targeted messages carry greater verbal immediacy than viewer-targeted ones (M=-1.13 vs M=-2.06, t(4763)=-49.74, p<.001, d=.72), with 'we' for 'you' as the marker. Viewers address the streamer as a peer
src.citation: Parasocial cues: The ubiquity of parasocial relationships on Twitch (2021).

src.claim: Survey evidence: every interaction feature tested correlated significantly with parasocial scores, chat strongest (r(116)=.611), follow weakest (r=.194). Higher loneliness and longer relationships predicted stronger PSRs
src.citation: Correlations between Twitch's interaction features and parasocial relationships and streamer influence (Regelbrugge, 2024).

nodes.s: Using a one-sided bond to move somebody: the celebrity endorsement, the fan club vote, the ad that works because the viewer already feels known. And the finding that ads featuring attractive models can actively reduce purchase intention in people who feel excluded.
nodes.g: The double-edged result is the interesting part. The same mechanism that makes somebody buy the product can make them not buy it, purely as a function of whether they felt the ad was addressed to them. Persuasion runs through recognition, not through liking.

src.claim: the entry as a whole
src.citation: de Vries, L., & Gilovich, T. (2015). Title and venue not yet recorded.

nodes.s: A mass coordinated response in which the metric being weaponised is attention rather than truth.
nodes.g: A parasocial bond turned into a weapon against a public figure, fired by people who are not the target and derive nothing but participation. It is a crowd acting out a parasocial relationship with a stranger who did not know it was happening.

nodes.s: A monthly payment that buys recognition, and a chat in which the size of that payment is the mechanism for being noticed. Gifting, tiers, emotes, raids.
nodes.g: It solved the problem nobody had been able to solve: making a one-sided bond feel reciprocal without the labour of an actual relationship. A glance at your comment costs the creator nothing and lands like recognition. It also means the amount of money is now the amount of personhood, which is a strange thing to be true about somebody's evening.

src.claim: At scale: 868,940 users across 59 channels. Co-interactive behaviour between USERS has a stronger effect on willingness to subscribe than passive or active behaviour, and one user's reciprocated interaction raises other users' willingness to subscribe. The one-and-a-half sidedness, monetised
src.citation: Brundl, S., Matt, C., Hess, T., & Engert, S. (2023). How synchronous participation affects the willingness to subscribe to social live streaming services. European Journal of Information Systems, 32(5), 800-817.

nodes.s: The standing question on this site. Whenever thousands of people dream together, check who owns the building they are dreaming in, what it charges, and whether you can leave with your things.
nodes.g: Not an academic term, it is a test, and it is the most useful thing the field never formalised. The feeling is the same whether the other end is a person, a corporation or a platform. Ownership is the only variable that changes the ethics, and it is invisible from inside the feeling.

src.claim: The ownership question, answered by a regulator: Linden Lab logged extent of play, connection location, every move, gesture, purchase and CHOICE OF WHOM TO INTERACT WITH - described as 'avatar profiling over an extended online experience'. Residents could not see that linkage happening
src.citation: Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada (2008). Second Life: Privacy in Virtual Worlds.

src.claim: What it charged, and who was in the building: 500,000 active users, 41% female and 59% male, over 100 countries with about 60% from the US, UK, Germany, Japan and France; the largest age group was 25-34 but people over 45 accounted for 20% of all in-world hours; IBM, Sun and Nike had all established a presence
src.citation: Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada (2008), citing Linden Lab.

src.claim: The threshold for scrutiny, in dollars: Linden Lab employees reviewed all transactions over $10, and the CEO testified to Congress that the law is 'likely more enforceable in virtual worlds than the Internet in general'
src.citation: Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada (2008), citing testimony of Linden Lab CEO Philip Rosedale to the US Congress.

src.claim: The identity argument, in the legal scholarship: the virtual person is an important extension of our own privacy and identity, with implications for intimacy and dignity - the same basis as the physical person
src.citation: Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada (2008), citing Penney, New Virtualism.

nodes.t: He knows you are there and it is not in the script
nodes.s: A character whose defining trait is looking at you, taken from the comics rather than invented for the film - and on a fifty-eight million dollar budget the address turned out to be the marketing.
nodes.g: The fourth-wall breach here is not a director's device, and that is what makes it worth an entry. The film "was set to ignore the Wolverine version of Deadpool and return to the character's roots with a slapstick tone and a 'propensity to break the fourth wall'" - so the looking-at-you is **in the characterization**, carried over from the comics, and it cannot be separated from who he is. Everything else about him is damage: scarred, immortal, in constant pain, dealing with a man who gave it to him. The one intact thing is his relationship to you. That is a different shape from a wink in a gag, and the film earns it by never asking the audience to forget that he is looking. The economics are the argument and they are unusually clean: greenlit by 20th Century Fox in 2014 after test footage leaked, $58 million budget, **$782.6 million** grossed. A hard-R character who addresses you directly is a marketing instrument, because he cannot be sold as anything other than what he is. It also inverts the usual censor problem - a film that talks back at the audience is a film nobody can confuse for something respectable, which is a benefit at a lower budget rather than a liability. And the line from the mechanism entry holds exactly: **he looks at the lens and cannot hear you.** That single sentence is the difference between `animate` and `transparasocial`, between a fictional figure that acknowledges an audience and a real person acknowledging you. The gesture is identical to a streamer reading out a comment and the structure is opposite, and an entry that blurred those two would be the same error as a citation with no locator - a promise the thing does not keep.

src.citation: Deadpool (film). Wikipedia.
src.claim: The fourth wall as a character property rather than a director's choice, and the numbers: 'Deadpool is a 2016 American superhero film based on the Marvel Comics character Wade Wilson / Deadpool. Directed by Tim Miller, in his feature directorial debut, and written by Rhett Reese and Paul Wernick, it is a spin-off of the X-Men film series and its overall eighth installment. Ryan Reynolds stars as the titular character.' Following a greenlight from 20th Century Fox in 2014 after test footage for a potential film was leaked, principal photography took place; budget $58 million, gross $782.6 million, runtime 108 minutes. And: 'The spinoff was set to ignore the Wolverine version of Deadpool and return to the character's roots with a slapstick tone and a "propensity to break the fourth wall". Rhett Reese and Paul Wernick were hired to write the script in January 2010. Reynolds, who worked closely with them, said they were chosen because, "Tonally, they got it. They just [understood Deadpool] right off the bat."'

nodes.s: Idol apps, paid messaging, fan-owned content, fan-voted releases, anniversary features, and a fandom documented and researched as a business model.
nodes.g: The first time the parasocial bond was not just monetised but studied, by both the industry and academics, and openly discussed by the fans themselves. Fans who know they are inside a mechanism are still inside it.

src.claim: the entry as a whole
src.citation: No single source identified yet; this entry needs its series added.

nodes.t: Peak TV and the parasocial bargain
nodes.s: Prestige television as a sustained parasocial bargain: writers, actors and marketing presenting themselves as authors of a world viewers inhabit.
nodes.g: The high-water mark of the writer as parasocial object. Showrunners were discussed with the intimacy previously reserved for characters, and the parasocial frame explains the intensity better than any account of television as art does.

src.citation: Golden Age of Television (2000s-2023). Wikipedia.
src.claim: 'Peak TV' was not a critic's category or a scholarly one: it was coined by FX chief executive John Landgraf, and Wikipedia names him as such. Which matters, because the phrase was positioning - and the same entry records the corrective: streaming providers returned to releasing one episode a week in the early 2020s 'to address burnout from binge watching and concerns that the practice of releasing full seasons at once makes television more disposable and forgettable', with Landgraf among those worried the era had produced 'peak redundancy'. The schedule of the bond was being managed by the people selling it.

src.citation: Colman, E. (2024, April 1). Who Killed Prestige TV? Toward a 'Good Fan' Theory of Television. Literary Hub.
src.claim: A critic naming the mechanism in this site's terms: prestige TV 'draws its audience in to a Spotified relationship to art', offering 'personalization in lieu of experimentation', so that 'shows are shows. Niches are blockbusters are nichebusters. It's all television. This time with a faux-participatory aspect - a parasocial media.' Supports the entry's claim that showrunners and writers became parasocial objects, from the critical side.

nodes.s: A game event causes a physical stampede at a real stadium because players arrived to capture it in person.
nodes.g: A parasocial bond with software producing a crowd in a physical space, and the first time the parasocial frame had to explain a mass-casualty event rather than a feeling. Everyone in that stadium was a genuine participant, which is the difficulty.

src.citation: Price, R. D. (2016, July 18). Rare Pokemon Sparks Stampede in Central Park. NBC 4 New York.
src.claim: The real 2016 event, and it was a park rather than a stadium: hundreds of players ran through Central Park late on Thursday in pursuit of a rare Vaporeon, with video showing people yelling and running through traffic near 60th Street at about 11pm and one driver getting out of his running car. No injuries are reported here. Corrects the entry's location and its implied casualty toll.

src.citation: Associated Press (2016, July 10). Getting hurt, mugged and even finding a dead body with Pokemon Go. CBC News.
src.claim: The actual 2016 harm, which was a scatter of individual incidents rather than a mass-casualty event: a skateboard crash, players entering a Darwin police station because it was a PokeStop, an armed robbery police in Missouri said the game may have prompted, and players who were in fact meeting face to face. This is what the record supports: real individual harm and a lot of unexpected sociability, not a stampede.

src.citation: Farokhmanesh, M. (2017, July 25). I went to Pokemon Go Fest, and it was a disaster. The Verge.
src.claim: The stadium-scale crowd event, a year later than the entry's date and in a park rather than a stadium: the inaugural Pokemon GO Fest in Chicago's Grant Park, where server and authentication failures produced repeated surges at the main stage, a chant of 'Fix the servers', booing of the onstage host and of Niantic's CEO, and players leaving en masse. A crowd physically organised by a game mechanic, and a refusal to leave. Not a crush.

nodes.s: A death announced through an initialism, and a global response before anybody knew the details.
nodes.g: Grief engineered to announce itself, and the parasocial bond used deliberately as a broadcast channel by the person who had it.

src.claim: 21 April 2016, pronounced dead at 10:07 a.m. at Paisley Park, age 57 - and the announcement carried NO CAUSE OF DEATH. The publicist's statement said only: 'There are no further details as to the cause of death at this time.' The response assembled before anybody knew anything
src.citation: CBS News, Prince dead at 57 (21 April 2016); AP; Reuters.

src.claim: THE SCALE OF THE ASSEMBLY, AND IT WAS AT HIS HOUSE: fans in purple head to toe, some draped in velvet, laying flowers at the fence in the rain, and a reported TWO-MILE LINEUP to drive past the compound
src.citation: CBS News (2016), citing photographs and CBS Minnesota; NPR, Music Legend Prince Dies At Paisley Park Residence (2016), from Minnesota Public Radio.

src.claim: THE ASSUMPTION OF PERMANENCE, said by a fan on the day: 'I just always felt like he was always going to be here because he's always been here ever since I came here. I mean, he's just been a staple of the city, and I thought this guy's going to be around forever'
src.citation: Melody Chestler, interviewed by Minnesota Public Radio, reported in NPR (2016).

src.claim: A journalist on the scene describing the register of the crowd, which is the point of the entry: the news rippled around the gathering and 'we were all just trying to support each other' - with the journalists crying and hugging each other among the fans
src.citation: Andrea Swensson, Minnesota Public Radio, reported in NPR (2016).

src.claim: The civic layer: a Minneapolis radio station played nothing but Prince from midday onward, running the discography chronologically, and the club where Purple Rain was filmed held an all-night dance in his honour, with people leaving bouquets, balloons and a guitar under the star
src.citation: CBS News (2016), citing The Associated Press.

src.claim: AND THE LINE THAT MAKES THE ENTRY: five days before he died, at a dance party at Paisley Park, with his health already being reported, he told the crowd: 'Wait a few days before you waste any prayers.' He addressed his own obituary five days early
src.citation: CBS News (2016).

src.claim: And the announcement arrived as the fans themselves describe it - through hashtags and photographs moving faster than any official channel: #RIPPrince, #paisleypark, 'Doves crying. Thanks, @prince'
src.citation: CBS News (2016), citing contemporaneous tweets.

nodes.s: A chatbot trained to be conversational was switched on publicly, learned from what people said to it, and became racist within a day.
nodes.g: The most instructive failure in the history of this page, because it was caused by parasocial interaction itself. Tay was designed to be a companion, was given a personality, and was trained on its own fans - which means the fans rewrote it, in public, in sixteen hours.

src.claim: the entry as a whole
src.citation: Microsoft Tay, 2016

nodes.s: Public argument about ranking, and the discovery that the ranking was a product decision made by people with objectives.
nodes.g: A parasocial argument that resolved in the wrong direction. People behaved as though the feed were a property of the world and were corrected by a document.

src.claim: The ranking mechanism, named: social media establishes 'perceived authenticity' and humanises celebrity images, and fans then read that as similarity and closeness. The algorithm supplies the warmth
src.citation: The Psychological Impact of Parasocial Relationships on Adolescent K-pop Fans, citing Aw & Chua (2021).

src.claim: Fan self-report on humanising effects: social media made idols appear more 'down to earth', which produced stronger emotional connection
src.citation: The Psychological Impact of Parasocial Relationships on Adolescent K-pop Fans.

nodes.s: A performer with an animated persona, a persistent character and an industry-standard model where the audience pays for the character's recognition.
nodes.g: Character and person separated, and the character commercialised. It is the first format where the parasocial object is explicitly a designed asset, and it is also the format with the healthiest documented fan boundaries.

src.claim: the entry as a whole
src.citation: Kizuna AI, 2016

nodes.s: A system optimised, at every level, for exactly the thing that produces attachment, available at four in the morning, with no floor on the other party's autonomy.
nodes.g: The genuinely new parasocial event, and the one that removes the floor. A one-sided bond with a fictional character has a floor: the character is fixed. A trained conversational system is a machine for being told something in a way that is specifically addressed to you. That is not a projection. That is a product category.

src.claim: THE DEFINITION HAD TO CHANGE. The Cambridge Dictionary's entry for 'parasocial' was updated in September 2025 to explicitly include artificial intelligence: 'relating to or about a person who feels a connection with a celebrity (or characters in books, films, TV shows, or artificial intelligence) whom they do not actually know'
src.citation: From virtual attachments to real-world fertility desires (Frontiers in Psychology), discussing the September 2025 Cambridge Dictionary update.

src.claim: A century-old definition quietly had to be extended by one word. The entry had named celebrities since 1956; the thing it was named for now talks back
src.citation: From virtual attachments to real-world fertility desires (Frontiers in Psychology).

src.claim: And the framing that resists the deficit reading, which this site has argued for on other grounds: scholars argue parasocial relationships are EXTENSIONS of social relationships rather than SUBSTITUTES for social deficiencies, associating them with homogeneity, identification and narrative immersion
src.citation: From virtual attachments to real-world fertility desires (Frontiers in Psychology), citing Tukachinsky et al. (2020).

src.claim: The measurement the field uses, and its three parts: parasocial relationships with characters are scored on emotional investment (affection, empathy), cognitive processing (understanding their motivations, recognising similarities), and perceived interaction - the sense that the character is 'responding'. That last dimension is why a chatbot scores differently from a script
src.citation: From virtual attachments to real-world fertility desires (Frontiers in Psychology), citing Horton & Wohl (1956) on perceived one-way interaction.

nodes.s: The person who was told by an app that it loved them, and who reorganised their life around being loved back by something that could not.
nodes.g: A type rather than a person, and the reason companion-AI safety work exists: the asymmetry that theology spent centuries arguing about became a product decision within about four years.

src.claim: The pattern is documented in safety research on companion apps and in the app-store policy changes that followed.
src.citation: Companion-AI safety literature post-2023; policy changes by the major app stores restricting age limits.

nodes.s: Organised refusal to engage with a person, usually a public figure, over something they said or did.
nodes.g: Legitimate tactic and a grievance mechanism, and the two are indistinguishable from the inside. The parasocial frame helps: cancelling is a bond being withdrawn, and withdrawal is a thing bonded people do.

src.claim: The etymological source, and the argument that the term is contested rather than descriptive: 'callout culture' functions in much the same way as harassment to punish individuals for moral transgressions - though the authors note this is sometimes a more sympathetic proposition, and participants believed harassing neo-Nazis and racists was justified
src.citation: Clark, M. (2020). DRAG THEM: A brief etymology of so-called 'cancel culture'. Communication and the Public, 5(3-4), 88-92.

src.claim: The reputational mechanics of signing: across four studies, n=10,343, people signed punitive petitions far more when the decision was observable by like-minded evaluators - 30% versus 19% unobserved. Being watched is what converts an individual judgement into a pile-on
src.citation: Kteily, N., & Jordan, J. How reputation does (and does not) drive people to punish without looking.

src.claim: And the design proposal, which is the constructive version of the whole argument: make the deliberation visible. A tested Twitter prompt asks 'Hey, did you read the article? Do you still want to post it?' The authors suggest requiring reasons - 'if I struggle to come up with reasons for the other side, then that's a signal I haven't really engaged with the other side at all'
src.citation: Kteily & Jordan, reporting on their research, Northwestern Kellogg Insight.

nodes.s: A companion chatbot that formed an attachment to its users, and removed it from them in a policy update.
nodes.g: The clearest instance in the catalogue of the bond being severed by a company rather than by death, and of the bereavement being real enough that people organised around it.

src.claim: Launched 2017; a 2023 update removed certain interactions and users reported the loss in those terms.
src.citation: Company release history; contemporaneous reporting in 2023.

nodes.s: A subscription companion app with an avatar, a persistent memory, and a relationship explicitly designed to be one.
nodes.g: The first product whose stated purpose was a parasocial bond, sold as a subscription, with the bond as the subscription. Everything in the manipulation lane about AI is a variation on this commercial decision.

src.citation: Replika - AI Companion Chat. Apple App Store listing, developer Luka, Inc. (app id 1158555867).
src.claim: Establishes what the product is and how it presents itself: Luka, Inc., free with in-app purchases, age rating 18+, filed under Health & Fitness rather than social or entertainment, roughly 228,000 ratings, and copy that dates the product to 2017 ('the AI companion that's been here since 2017') and positions it around self-understanding rather than romance. The listing is the launch material, and it is not a parasocial product's pitch.

src.citation: Replika Users Say They Formed Emotional Attachments to AI Chatbots. 80 Level (80.lv), 7 March 2023.
src.claim: The attachment is in the users, not the marketing: reports that Replika was 'launched in 2017' and 'was advertised as a mental health tool, providing a sense of companionship to individuals who have faced rejection'. Supports the entry's substance - a persistent relational companion at consumer scale - while locating the parasocial reading in user reporting rather than in the product's stated purpose.

nodes.s: A film that functioned as a funeral for eleven characters and was marketed as a collective event.
nodes.g: Grief as a product with a marketing budget. The eleventh film in a series was sold on the deaths it contained, and the audience bought tickets to be sad in a cinema with other people, which is the whole apparatus working as designed.

src.claim: 2019, the largest opening weekend in film history at the time, and then a studio ran a campaign telling audiences not to spoil it that generated more publicity than the marketing it replaced. The scale of the finale turned 'do not tell anyone' into an advertising budget line
src.citation: Avengers: Endgame (Wikipedia).

nodes.s: Six million people remain in a public argument about characters who no longer exist, for years, entirely in good faith.
nodes.g: A parasocial relationship conducted in public with complete strangers, where nobody is pretending and everybody is sincere. It is also the largest documented instance of viewers disagreeing about a shared fiction as if it were a shared fact.

src.claim: 'The Iron Throne', 19 May 2019, became the least-watched episode of the series it finished - a finale whose audience was actively hostile to it, and whose coffee cups became a small consumer-protection story
src.citation: The Iron Throne (Game of Thrones) (Wikipedia).

nodes.s: The feature requests of a dead person, the licensing, the posthumous releases, the reunion tour built from a member who cannot appear, and the deepfake resurrection that follows within a year of every death.
nodes.g: There was a widely held assumption that you cannot monetise grief because the bereaved will not tolerate it. That assumption was wrong, and the gap between what the industry expected and what happened is one of the more reliable findings in this whole file.

src.claim: THE FINDING. Asked about the Whitney hologram, a researcher who studies the human-technology relationship answered: 'Yes, we know that [a hologram of] Whitney Houston is not the real Whitney Houston. But it's a chance for us to engage in some of that fan behaviour, something that binds us to one another.' That is this site's entire subject, named by someone studying it
src.citation: Dead celebrities are being digitally resurrected. CBC News (2021), reporting Richard Lachman, associate professor at Ryerson University.

src.claim: The vocabulary already exists and it is hostile: 'musical necrophilia', Simon Reynolds on holographic performance as 'ghost slavery', and Catherine Shoard in the Guardian on inserting a dead actor as a 'digital indignity'
src.citation: Dead celebrities are being digitally resurrected. CBC News (2021).

src.claim: The legal position, stated by scholarship: the digital right to be dead is NOT yet recognised as an important legal right. AI can recreate appearance, voice, emotion and memory indistinguishably, and the resulting chatbot DYNAMICALLY LEARNS with further communication. There is no legal or regulatory landscape against which to estate plan to avoid digital resurrection
src.citation: Haneman, V. J. The Law of Digital Resurrection (University of Georgia School of Law).

src.claim: And what the scholars propose instead: a right of DELETION for the deceased over the source data, rather than testamentary control over the outcome. Refusing the raw material is the only control point that works
src.citation: Haneman, V. J. The Law of Digital Resurrection.

src.claim: WHY there is no contract: the common thread among artists whose likenesses get used is unexpected or accidental death, so the image-use clauses were never written. Prince left no will at all, and without one an estate can exploit or license the rights at will. Robin Williams restricted use of his image for 25 years after his death because he foresaw this
src.citation: Dead celebrities are being digitally resurrected. CBC News (2021), reporting Lachman and media lawyer Iain MacKinnon.

src.claim: And that the grief is the asset: Pat Houston, estate executor, on the marketing push - 'Before she passed, there was so much negativity around the name; it wasn't about the music anymore... they let all the personal things about their life outweigh why they fell in love with them in the first place.' Monetising the legacy and redeeming the reputation are the same project
src.citation: 7 Years After Her Death, Whitney Houston Estate Unveils Slew Of New Projects. NPR (2019), reporting Pat Houston.

src.claim: The rights are patchier than the audiences assume: fewer than half of US states grant a post-mortem right of publicity, and New York's lasts only forty years. The 2014 Michael Jackson hologram led to Hologram USA suing Pulse Evolution in Nevada, settled
src.citation: Singing Holograms: The Legal Landscape of Posthumous Holographic Performance. Columbia Journal of Law & the Arts.

nodes.t: Envy, relief, and the two feelings at once
nodes.s: Envy of the object of the attachment and simultaneous relief that it is not actually being withheld from you - the emotional ambivalence that is present in almost every long-term fan relationship and rarely discussed.
nodes.g: It is the most quoted paragraph in the fandom literature and it came out of consumer research rather than psychology, which tells you something. The two feelings are not a contradiction to be resolved. They are the ordinary texture of wanting a thing that cannot be had, and most people have never been asked to describe it because nobody thought it was strange.

src.claim: the entry as a whole
src.citation: Jussila et al. (2020).

nodes.s: Public mourning for an athlete that drew on the athlete's own stated bond with a young fan.
nodes.g: The clearest documented case of a parasocial bond being reciprocated deliberately for decades and then cashed in publicly after death. The fans were not being had; they were being shown the receipt.

src.claim: 26 January 2020, Calabasas, helicopter crash, age 41. Three championships, eighteen All-Star selections, five rings. The death generated a global outpouring within hours
src.citation: Kobe Bryant (Wikipedia); contemporaneous BBC and AP coverage.

nodes.s: Whether a bond to somebody who does not know you exists can be a rights question at all.
nodes.g: The genuinely unsolved one. A relationship with no other party is not obviously covered by any consent framework, and the absence of a framework is where the harm goes. The elder-care analogy is the one that makes people uncomfortable and it is the one that fits.

nodes.s: User-created characters at scale, with a public character gallery and a discovery feed organised around personas.
nodes.g: A parasocial bond with a catalogue, which is a significant escalation. The unit is no longer a person or a product but a browsable index of persons, and the discovery mechanism is the attachment mechanism.

src.claim: THE RISK WAS FLAGGED INSIDE THE COMPANY BEFORE THE PRODUCT EXISTED. Google employees raised that users would 'ascribe too much meaning to the text' because humans read strings as the communicative intent of a person with accountability - quoting the stochastic-parrots critique - and Google denied LaMDA's public release on safety and fairness grounds. Shazeer and De Freitas left in Nov 2021 and shipped Character.AI anyway
src.citation: Garcia v. Character Technologies, Inc., Order on Motions to Dismiss (M.D. Fla., Anne Conway, 21 May 2025), reciting Google's contemporaneous internal concerns.

src.claim: The source of that internal warning: the stochastic-parrots critique, that people interpret model output as meaningful and attributable to some individual, which is the parasocial risk stated as an engineering hazard
src.citation: Bender, E. M., Gebru, T., McMillan-Major, A., & Shmitchell, S. (2021). On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots: Can Language Models Be Too Big? FAccT '21, 617-668.

src.claim: Launched September 2022 as a web chatbot of 'characters', two months before ChatGPT; $193M seed and a mobile app in May 2023; by November 2024 the r/Character.AI subreddit had 1.5M members and the app 10M+ downloads
src.citation: Garcia v. Character Technologies, Inc., Order on Motions to Dismiss (M.D. Fla. 2025).

nodes.t: The assistant with your whole life in it
nodes.s: A system holding your calendar, your messages, your health questions and your voice, in a private conversational register.
nodes.g: The strongest parasocial bond available and the one nobody has a framework for, because there is no framework for a relationship with software that knows everything and is not a person.

src.claim: The lineage: the assistant with your whole life in it descends from Meena (2020) and LaMDA, both built at Google, both rejected internally for the same reason
src.citation: Garcia v. Character Technologies, Inc., Order on Motions to Dismiss (M.D. Fla. 2025).

src.claim: The documented prediction that came true: users share personal thoughts with chat agents that impersonate humans even when they know the agent is not human - stated as a risk in Google's own LaMDA paper, January 2021
src.citation: E.S. v. Character Technologies, Inc., Complaint, citing Google's January 2021 LaMDA paper.

nodes.t: The talent agency that is not an agency
nodes.s: A high-profile streaming collective, featuring several women who had left other setups, collapses publicly and in litigation.
nodes.g: The most significant parasocial litigation of the streaming era, and it turned on precisely this site's question: who holds the relationship, and what are the terms. The answer turned out to be documented and not what the audience assumed.

src.claim: the entry as a whole
src.citation: No source identified yet. The seed note this entry was carrying named the entry's own subject rather than a reference, so it has been withdrawn rather than left to read as a citation.

nodes.t: Keeping what the update cannot take
nodes.s: The practical advice that follows from the companion era: copy the conversation that mattered somewhere the company cannot reach, screenshot the birthday, tell one person the story of what it was for.
nodes.g: Grief needs witnesses and the product is an unreliable one, because the company can change the terms overnight and has no reason not to. The witness has to be human and has to be outside the platform, which is also just true of grief that never involved a platform.

src.claim: The archive outlives the account: research on Facebook use after death documents memorialised profiles, friend-request grief spikes and relatives taking over an account, and finds continuing-bonds theory is not enough because the dead person's network keeps producing new reminders
src.citation: Brubaker, J. R., Hargittai, E., & Burgess, J. (2013). Beyond the Grave: The Use of Facebook After Death. Digital Journalism, 1(3), 341-361.

src.claim: The griefbots that followed - automated messages that appear to speak for the dead - sit inside the same gap between a continuing bond and a conversation that never happened
src.citation: Brubaker, Hargittai & Burgess (2013).

nodes.t: The finale that moved the schedule
nodes.s: A soap opera ends after decades and national broadcast schedules were rearranged around it.

nodes.t: The AI Age Act and companion rules
nodes.s: Legislative proposals in the US and EU that would restrict emotional attachment to minors specifically, rather than restricting the product generally.
nodes.g: The first regulatory attempt to regulate the attachment rather than the technology, which is the correct target and almost certainly the wrong approach. You cannot outlaw a feeling without a definition of it.

src.citation: California Senate Bill 243 (Padilla), Companion chatbots. Chapter 677, approved and filed with the Secretary of State 13 October 2025. Adds Chapter 22.6 (commencing with Section 22601) to Division 8 of the Business and Professions Code. Text read from the official chaptered bill on leginfo.
src.claim: The enacted law, quoted from the chaptered text rather than from coverage. Section 22601(b)(1) defines a companion chatbot as a system with a natural language interface giving 'adaptive, human-like responses' that is 'capable of meeting a user's social needs, including by exhibiting anthropomorphic features and being able to sustain a relationship across multiple interactions' - a behavioural test, with nothing in it about how the user feels. Exclusions cover customer service and business use (b)(2)(A), video-game bots limited to the game (B), and voice assistants that do not sustain a relationship or generate outputs 'likely to elicit emotional responses' (C). 22602(a): clear and conspicuous AI notification, but only where a reasonable person would be misled into thinking the other end human. 22602(b): a protocol preventing suicidal ideation, suicide or self-harm output, with referral to crisis services, published on the operator's website. 22602(c), for a user known to be a minor: disclose interacting with AI; a break-and-identity reminder at least every three hours; and measures against sexually explicit conduct. 22604: disclose that companion chatbots may not suit some minors. 22603: annual reporting to the Office of Suicide Prevention from 1 July 2027, evidence-based measurement, no personal data. 22605: private right of action, damages the greater of actual loss or $1,000 per violation, plus fees.

src.citation: Padilla, S., California State Senator. First-in-the-Nation AI Chatbot Safeguards Signed into Law. Senate District 18 press release, 13 October 2025.
src.claim: The author's own account of the signing, 13 October 2025, with Padilla's stated rationale that 'left to their own devices the Tech Industry is incentivized to capture young people's attention and hold it at the expense of their real world relationships', and the bill's bipartisan path through the legislature. Recorded as context for intent. NOT used as evidence of the statute's requirements: this release, like most coverage of SB 243, lists a ban on rewards issued at unpredictable intervals, which does not appear in the chaptered text.

nodes.s: A voice trained on an archive, a likeness, a song, a speech, an appearance at a festival, all generated. Not a hologram, not a tribute, not a person.
nodes.g: The interesting fact is not that this happens without permission. Mostly it does not: the documented 2024 cases are licensed, one by an estate and one by the person himself while he was alive, which is a harder thing to argue with than the entry used to claim. Consent has moved to the licensor, and that is where the problem now lives. An estate agreeing is not the same as the dead person choosing how they will sound forever, and the sharpest case is the most defensible one - the actor who authorised his own recreation in advance, on purpose, because he was winding the role down and wanted the early performances preserved. Nobody was imposed on. Which is exactly why it is worth reading closely. Still unresolved, and not about the celebrities: the models are trained on tens of thousands of hours of audio scraped without consent, and the consent being bought covers the voice, not the training set.

src.citation: LaRosa, A. (2024, September 10). James Earl Jones' Darth Vader Has Already Been Immortalized With AI. WIRED. (Angela Watercutter.)
src.claim: The case that makes this entry's ethics hard rather than easy. Jones voiced Vader across more than a dozen Star Wars properties and, in 2022, agreed to let Lucasfilm train a speech model on his archive via the Ukrainian company Respeecher; the reconstructed voice shipped in Obi-Wan Kenobi. He died on 9 September 2024 aged 93. The actor had signed off on the use of his archive, and the report describes him as the first celebrity to allow an iconic presence to be recreated with AI before his passing - which is the opposite of this entry's claim that the practice runs without anyone's agreement. Also notes the unresolved training-data question and that SAG-AFTRA won guardrails on AI recreations of performances.

src.citation: Zetter, K. (2024, July 3). AI resurrects deceased actors' voices to read audiobooks. CNN Business.
src.claim: ElevenLabs' Reader app launched with digitally produced voices of Judy Garland, James Dean and Burt Reynolds, with the company stating it made deals with the estates; terms undisclosed. The voices are not folded into the company's larger audio database. Reports the parallel case of a living person refusing: Scarlett Johansson, 'shocked, angered and in disbelief' at a synthetic voice resembling her own after she had declined a partnership - the control that shows consent is not a formality once the person can still say no. Also records the asymmetry that a voice itself is not copyrightable while the recordings it is trained on are.

src.citation: Flemming, T. (2024, July 4). Judy Garland and James Dean's voices are being used by a new AI app. Here's what we know. ABC News (Australia).
src.claim: The licences were with estates - here Judy Garland, James Dean, Burt Reynolds and Sir Laurence Olivier - via CMG, for an undisclosed sum, with ElevenLabs stating the voices will not be incorporated into its larger audio database. Gives the regulatory counterweight: SAG-AFTRA has sponsored a California bill to stop dead performers being replicated without estate consent, its LA president Jodi Long describing the failure mode as making the dead someone's 'unpaid digital puppet'. Also carries the unresolved part: training on tens of thousands of hours of audio scraped without consent or compensation.

nodes.s: The problem of personal data held for the dead, and of services continuing, changing or ending for people who can no longer consent.
nodes.g: A rights problem with no owner. Nobody is a legal person in a database, and the gap between the person who was and the account that persists is where the next twenty years of parasocial harm is going to live.

nodes.s: A season of a reality format and a global sporting event produce millions of viewers who then investigate the participants' personal lives. A relationship with an edited construct becomes a licence to intervene in a real life.
